hydration.title: Hydration
hydration.intro: Water is the lever almost nobody measures — yet a 1–2% drop in body water visibly dents focus, mood, and physical output. This track gives you a real daily target, the electrolytes that make water actually work, and a way to read your own status.

lessons.title: Why hydration is a lever, not a vibe
lessons.summary: What water actually does, and what mild dehydration costs you.

blocks.body:
You are roughly **60% water** by mass. It's the solvent every reaction runs in, the coolant for your temperature, the medium that carries nutrients in and waste out, and the cushion around your brain and joints. None of that is optional — which is why your body defends water balance aggressively.

The catch: thirst lags behind need. By the time you feel thirsty you're already mildly dehydrated, and the early cost shows up not as a dry mouth but as **worse thinking and mood**.

blocks.label: Drop in body water linked to measurable dips in concentration, alertness, and mood — a deficit you can reach before you feel thirsty.
blocks.source: Dehydration studies & meta-analyses (effects clearest above ~2%; size varies by task)

blocks.title: Thirst is a late signal
blocks.body: Thirst kicks in around the point where performance is already dipping. Don't use it as your only cue — anchor intake to a daily target and your urine color instead.

blocks.question: What's usually the FIRST noticeable effect of mild (1–2%) dehydration?
options: Muscle cramps
Dips in focus, alertness, and mood
A spike in blood pressure
Nothing until you're 5%+ down
blocks.explanation: Mood and attention effects tend to show up first and at small deficits — typically before cramps or obvious physical symptoms. That's why hydration is a daily-performance lever, not just an exercise concern.

lessons.title: How much water do you actually need?
lessons.summary: A real per-bodyweight target — and why the '8 glasses' rule is a myth.

blocks.body: The famous "8 glasses a day" has no real scientific basis — it ignores that you're a different size from everyone else, and that **food and other drinks count too** (about 20% of intake typically comes from food). A better baseline scales with your body.

blocks.prompt: Roughly how much TOTAL water (from drinks + food) does a 70 kg / 154 lb adult need on an average day?
blocks.explanation: A common, defensible baseline is about **35 mL per kg of body weight** per day of total water. For 70 kg that's ~2.45 L. Roughly 80% comes from drinks and 20% from food. Heat, exercise, altitude, illness, caffeine, alcohol, and high-protein or high-salt diets all push the number up.

blocks.title: Where 35 mL/kg comes from
blocks.simple: Bigger bodies hold and turn over more water, so a per-kilogram rule fits better than a fixed number of glasses. ~35 mL/kg/day is a sensible starting point you then adjust for heat and activity.
blocks.mechanism: Daily water turnover is driven by obligatory losses: urine (to excrete the solute load from food), insensible loss through skin and breath, and sweat. These scale with body size, metabolic rate, and environment. Per-kg targets approximate that turnover; the kidneys then fine-tune by concentrating or diluting urine via ADH (vasopressin).
blocks.studies: The U.S. National Academies set an adequate intake (for young adults) of ~3.7 L/day total water for men and ~2.7 L for women from ALL sources — figures that already include water from food and that vary with body size and activity. The 35 mL/kg rule is a practical per-bodyweight approximation that lands in a similar range and matches observed adult water turnover. There's no high-quality evidence that pushing far beyond your needs improves health in well-hydrated people; the benefit is in avoiding a deficit, not in 'over-drinking.'

blocks.body: Don't try to chug your whole target at once — the kidneys can only process so much per hour, and you'll just pee it out. Spread intake across the day.

blocks.title: Your water target

blocks.label: See your hydration target in the app
blocks.body: Formulate estimates your personal target from your body weight and shows today's intake against it.

lessons.title: Electrolytes — water needs a wingman
lessons.summary: Sodium, potassium, magnesium and chloride are what let water do its job.

blocks.body: Drinking plain water isn't the whole story. Water follows **electrolytes** — charged minerals that set the osmotic gradients controlling where fluid goes. Drink a lot of plain water while low on sodium and you can actually dilute your blood, which is both ineffective and, in extremes, dangerous.

blocks.title: The four electrolytes that matter most

nodes.label: Sodium (Na⁺)
nodes.detail: The main driver of fluid balance in the blood and between cells. You lose it in sweat — which is why heavy sweating needs salt, not just water. It also powers nerve signaling.

nodes.label: Potassium (K⁺)
nodes.detail: The dominant electrolyte INSIDE cells; it balances sodium. Higher potassium intake (from fruit, vegetables, legumes) supports healthy blood pressure. Most people get too little.

nodes.label: Magnesium (Mg²⁺)
nodes.detail: A cofactor for hundreds of enzymes (300+ by the classic estimate), including the sodium-potassium pumps that maintain the gradients. Commonly under-consumed; low magnesium is linked to more cramping and poorer sleep.

nodes.label: Chloride (Cl⁻)
nodes.detail: Sodium's partner anion; together they're most of your extracellular charge. It also makes stomach acid. Usually covered automatically when sodium and diet are adequate.

blocks.question: You did a long, sweaty workout in the heat. What's the smartest rehydration move?
options: Drink as much plain water as you can, fast
Replace fluid AND sodium (and ideally potassium)
Only worry about it if you cramp
Sip a sugary soda — the sugar is what matters
blocks.explanation: Sweat contains a lot of sodium. Replacing only water dilutes your remaining electrolytes and can leave you feeling worse. Add sodium (and some potassium) — that's the entire point of electrolyte/sports drinks for hard or hot sessions.

blocks.body: For everyday hydration with normal meals, you don't need an electrolyte product — food covers it. Reach for one around **heavy sweating, heat, illness with fluid loss, or fasting.**

lessons.title: Read your own hydration
lessons.summary: Simple, free signals that beat any rule of thumb.

blocks.body: You don't need a lab. Two free signals, thirst and the colour of your urine, tell you most of what you need, in real time.

blocks.title: Urine color is your dashboard
blocks.body: Aim for **pale straw / light yellow.** Dark amber means drink more; completely clear all day can mean you're over-doing plain water (or just diluting — back off slightly and consider electrolytes). Note: B-vitamins can turn urine bright yellow and throw this off.

blocks.title: Your daily hydration habits
items: Front-load a glass of water with each meal — three easy wins, automatically spaced.
Keep a bottle in sight; visibility drives intake more than willpower.
Add sodium/electrolytes around heavy sweat, heat, illness, or fasting.
Check urine color once midday — adjust the rest of the day from there.
Count coffee and tea — in moderation they hydrate too; the diuretic effect is mild.

blocks.label: Log your water and track the trend
blocks.body: Logging hydration turns these habits into a streak you can actually see.

lessons.title: Hydration for exercise & heat
lessons.summary: Estimate your sweat rate, replace what you lose, and know when water alone is enough.

blocks.body:
Exercise and heat are where hydration stops being a background lever and starts limiting performance. You can lose **0.5 to 2+ litres of sweat per hour** — and once you're down about 2% of body mass in fluid, endurance, power, and your sense of effort all start to slide.

The goal isn't to drink as much as possible. It's to roughly **match what you lose** — fluid and the sodium that leaves with it — without over-drinking.

blocks.prompt: During hard exercise in the heat, how much sweat can an average adult lose PER HOUR?
blocks.explanation: Sweat rates of **0.5–2+ litres per hour** are typical, with hot conditions, high intensity, and larger or heat-acclimatized people at the upper end. That's why you can't reliably out-drink a long hot session by feel alone — estimating your own rate beats guessing.

blocks.title: Estimate your sweat rate in one session
blocks.body: Weigh yourself (minimal clothing) before and after a ~1-hour workout. Every **1 kg lost ≈ 1 litre of sweat**. Add back any fluid you drank during the session. Example: down 0.8 kg + drank 500 mL = ~1.3 L sweat lost that hour. Do this a few times across conditions and you'll know your range.

blocks.title: How much sodium leaves in sweat — and why it matters
blocks.simple: Sweat is salty. The harder and longer you sweat, the more sodium you lose, and replacing only water can leave you flat or even unwell.
blocks.mechanism: Sweat sodium concentration varies a lot between people — roughly **0.5 to 1.5+ grams of sodium per litre** of sweat (about 1.3–3.8 g of salt). 'Salty sweaters' (white residue on skin/clothes, salty-tasting sweat) sit high. Lose 2 L of sweat and you can shed 1–3 g of sodium. If you replace that volume with plain water, blood sodium concentration falls — blunting the thirst and fluid-retention signals and, in extreme over-drinking, risking hyponatremia.
blocks.studies: Sport-science position stands (e.g. from major exercise and dietetics bodies) converge on: for sessions under ~60–90 minutes at moderate intensity, plain water and normal meals are usually adequate. For longer, hotter, or repeated same-day sessions — and for known salty/heavy sweaters — adding **sodium** (and replacing fluid to within a few percent of losses) improves rehydration and reduces the late-race performance drop. Carbohydrate (~30–60 g/hr) becomes useful mainly past ~60–90 minutes of hard effort, for fuel rather than hydration.

blocks.title: Before / during / after
items: **Before:** Arrive hydrated — pale-straw urine. ~400–600 mL in the 2–3 hours prior is plenty; no need to pre-load excessively.
**During:** For sessions under ~60 min in mild conditions, drink to thirst with water. For longer/hot sessions, sip ~400–800 mL/hr with sodium.
**After:** Replace ~125–150% of the fluid you lost (because you keep peeing) and include sodium + a meal to lock it in.
Weigh in occasionally pre/post to calibrate — don't rely on thirst for long hot efforts.

blocks.question: You're doing a 45-minute moderate run in mild weather. What's the sensible hydration plan?
options: Force down 1 L of electrolyte drink during the run
Drink to thirst with water; electrolytes aren't necessary for this
Drink nothing until you finish, then chug
Take salt tablets every 15 minutes
blocks.explanation: For short-to-moderate sessions in mild conditions, plain water to thirst plus normal meals covers it. The case for added sodium and carbs grows with duration, heat, and repeated sessions — not for a single sub-hour run.

blocks.label: Track your hydration around training
blocks.body: Logging intake on training days makes it obvious whether you're actually replacing what you sweat out.

lessons.title: Beverages compared
lessons.summary: What every common drink actually does for hydration — caffeine, sugar, and alcohol included.

blocks.body:
"Does coffee count?" is the most common hydration question — and the answer surprises people. Almost every drink hydrates you; what separates them is what *else* comes along: caffeine, sugar, or alcohol.

Hydration value isn't all-or-nothing. Researchers even rank drinks on how much fluid your body retains over the following hours — and milk and oral-rehydration-style drinks actually beat plain water on that measure, because the sodium and other nutrients slow how fast you pee it out.

blocks.title: Common drinks, ranked by what they bring

nodes.label: Water
nodes.detail: The baseline. Hydrates fully, zero calories, zero downside. The default for most of your daily intake.

nodes.label: Coffee & tea
nodes.detail: **Net hydrating** in normal amounts. Caffeine is a mild diuretic, but the fluid in the cup more than offsets it — habitual drinkers also adapt. Watch added sugar/syrups, not the water.

nodes.label: Milk
nodes.detail: Surprisingly **more hydrating than water** over the next few hours — its protein, fat, sodium, and potassium slow gastric emptying and urine output. Also a real source of protein and calcium.

nodes.label: Sports drinks
nodes.detail: Water + sodium + sugar (carbs). Genuinely useful for long/hot exercise; mostly **unnecessary sugar** if you're sitting at a desk. Right tool, wrong setting for everyday sipping.

nodes.label: Soda & juice
nodes.detail: Hydrate, but carry a **large sugar load** — a single can/glass can be 25–40 g sugar. Juice has some nutrients; soda is essentially sweetened water. Occasional, not a hydration strategy.

nodes.label: Alcohol
nodes.detail: **Net dehydrating.** It suppresses ADH (the hormone that tells kidneys to retain water), so you lose more fluid than the drink provides — especially with spirits. Alternate with water.

blocks.title: Why caffeine's diuretic effect barely matters
blocks.simple: Caffeine makes you pee a little more, but the water in your coffee or tea more than makes up for it — so the cup is still a net plus for hydration.
blocks.mechanism: Caffeine modestly increases urine output by blocking adenosine receptors in the kidney and slightly raising renal blood flow. But the effect is small at typical doses and the volume of fluid consumed alongside it is large. Regular caffeine users also develop partial tolerance to the diuretic response, shrinking it further.
blocks.studies: Controlled trials comparing caffeinated and non-caffeinated beverages have repeatedly found **no meaningful difference in 24-hour hydration status** at moderate caffeine intakes (roughly up to ~3–4 mg/kg, i.e. a few cups of coffee). The old advice to subtract coffee from your water total is outdated. A genuinely large single dose on a non-habituated person can produce a transient diuretic effect — but for everyday moderate drinkers, coffee and tea count toward fluid intake.

blocks.label: Sugar in a typical can of soda or large glass of juice — roughly a day's worth of added sugar in one drink, with no satiety to offset it.
blocks.source: Typical product nutrition labels (varies by brand and size)

blocks.question: Which of these is genuinely NET dehydrating?
options: A cup of black coffee
A glass of milk
A beer or glass of wine
Plain water
blocks.explanation: Alcohol suppresses ADH (vasopressin), so you excrete more fluid than the drink supplies — the only common beverage that's reliably net dehydrating. Coffee is net hydrating in moderation, and milk is actually retained longer than plain water.

blocks.body: If you drink alcohol, the simplest defense is **one glass of water between drinks** — it paces you, replaces some of the ADH-driven fluid loss, and softens the next morning.

lessons.title: Over- and under-hydration
lessons.summary: Dehydration signs by stage, the real danger of over-drinking, and who's most at risk.

blocks.body: Hydration is a balance, and you can err in **both** directions. Under-drinking is far more common; over-drinking is rarer but, in the wrong situation, more dangerous. Knowing the signs of each — and who's vulnerable — is what "getting it right" actually means.

blocks.title: Dehydration by stage

nodes.label: Mild (~1–2% body mass lost)
nodes.detail: Thirst, darker urine, slight drop in focus, alertness, and mood. Often unnoticed — this is the everyday deficit most people live in by mid-afternoon.

nodes.label: Moderate (~3–5%)
nodes.detail: Clear thirst, dry mouth, headache, fatigue, reduced urine, noticeable dip in physical and mental performance. Common after hard exercise or a hot day without enough fluid.

nodes.label: Severe (~6%+)
nodes.detail: Dizziness, rapid heartbeat, confusion, very little/dark urine, possible fainting. A medical situation — needs prompt rehydration, sometimes IV fluids.

blocks.title: Hyponatremia — when too much water is the problem
blocks.simple: Drinking far more plain water than you need, faster than your kidneys can clear it, can dilute the sodium in your blood to dangerous levels. It's rare but serious.
blocks.mechanism: Sodium sets the osmotic balance of your blood. If you pour in large volumes of plain water — beyond the kidney's excretion ceiling of roughly 0.8–1 L per hour — blood sodium concentration falls (hyponatremia). Water then moves into cells to equalize osmolarity, including brain cells, causing swelling. Symptoms climb from nausea, headache, and confusion to seizures and, in extreme cases, death. Heavy sweating that loses sodium, then replacing only with water, compounds it.
blocks.studies: Exercise-associated hyponatremia is documented mainly in **endurance events** (marathons, ultra-distance, long triathlons) where participants over-drink for hours — historically more common since the (now-outdated) 'drink as much as possible' era. The corrective guidance from sports-medicine consensus is to **drink to thirst** rather than to a forced schedule, and to include sodium on long efforts. Outside endurance sport, dangerous over-drinking is uncommon but can occur with certain psychiatric conditions, some medications, and water-loading challenges.

blocks.title: Who's most at risk
blocks.body: **Under-hydration:** older adults (blunted thirst), young children, anyone ill with vomiting/diarrhea/fever, and people in heat. **Over-hydration / hyponatremia:** endurance athletes who drink for hours, people on certain medications (e.g. some diuretics, SSRIs, the drug ecstasy), and anyone with kidney, heart, or hormonal conditions affecting fluid balance. If you're in either group, be more deliberate — and check with a clinician about your fluid and sodium needs.

blocks.question: A marathon runner collapses after drinking large amounts of PLAIN water throughout the race. The likeliest issue is:
options: Severe dehydration
Hyponatremia (diluted blood sodium)
Too much caffeine
Low blood sugar only
blocks.explanation: Hours of over-drinking plain water while losing sodium in sweat can dilute blood sodium — exercise-associated hyponatremia. The fix isn't 'more water'; it's drinking to thirst and including sodium on long efforts. This is why over-drinking can be as risky as under-drinking in endurance settings.

blocks.body: ⚕️ Severe dehydration (confusion, fainting, no urine) and suspected hyponatremia (worsening headache, nausea, confusion after heavy water intake) are **medical emergencies** — seek care rather than self-treating. This track is education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: Hydration, brain & body
lessons.summary: What good hydration actually does for cognition, headaches, skin, kidneys, and digestion — honestly.

blocks.body:
Hydration gets credited for everything from glowing skin to a sharper mind. Some of those claims are well-supported; others are oversold. This lesson separates the two so you know what to actually expect from drinking enough.

The honest headline: the clearest benefits come from **avoiding a deficit**, not from pushing fluid above your needs. Most effects on thinking and performance are reliable once you're past roughly **2% body-water loss**; below that they're real but smaller and noisier.

blocks.title: Where hydration helps — and how strong the evidence is

nodes.label: Cognition & mood
nodes.detail: **Solid above ~2% loss.** Attention, short-term memory, reaction time, and mood measurably worsen when dehydrated and recover with fluid. Effects at smaller deficits are real but more variable. Drinking *extra* beyond hydrated doesn't make you smarter.

nodes.label: Headaches
nodes.detail: **Plausible, individual.** Dehydration is a recognized headache trigger for some people; rehydrating can relieve a dehydration headache. Not every headache is fluid-related — but it's a cheap first thing to rule out.

nodes.label: Skin
nodes.detail: **Modest.** Severe dehydration reduces skin turgor, and very low intake may slightly affect skin hydration. But drinking gallons won't transform normal skin — topical and overall health matter more. Claims here are routinely overstated.

nodes.label: Kidneys & stones
nodes.detail: **Well-supported.** Higher fluid intake dilutes urine and is one of the most evidence-backed ways to **reduce kidney-stone recurrence** in stone-formers. Good hydration also eases the kidneys' workload.

nodes.label: Digestion & constipation
nodes.detail: **Supportive, especially with fiber.** Adequate fluid helps stool stay soft; low intake contributes to constipation. Water works *with* fiber — fiber without fluid can backfire.

blocks.title: Why the '2% threshold' keeps coming up
blocks.simple: Small fluid losses are buffered by your body, so effects are subtle. Once you cross about 2% of body weight in water lost, the buffering runs out and performance reliably drops.
blocks.mechanism: Your body defends blood volume and osmolarity first. Early losses are absorbed by shifting water between compartments and concentrating urine, so function holds. As deficit grows, blood volume and plasma osmolarity move enough to affect thermoregulation, cardiovascular strain, and brain function — which is why measurable cognitive and physical decrements cluster above ~2% body-mass loss.
blocks.studies: Meta-analyses of dehydration and cognition find consistent impairments to attention, executive function, and motor coordination at body-water deficits of roughly **2% and above**, with effect sizes that vary by task and how dehydration was induced. Below 2%, findings are mixed — some studies show small effects, others none — which is exactly why honest framing matters: the lever is real, but its size is modest at everyday deficits and it doesn't reverse into a bonus from over-drinking. For kidney stones, randomized and observational evidence for high fluid intake reducing recurrence is among the strongest in this whole list.

blocks.label: Body-mass loss above which dehydration's effects on focus, mood, and physical performance become reliably measurable. Below it, effects are real but smaller and noisier.

blocks.question: Which hydration benefit has the STRONGEST evidence behind it?
options: Drinking extra water makes skin visibly younger
More fluid reduces kidney-stone recurrence in stone-formers
Over-drinking boosts IQ
Water cures all headaches
blocks.explanation: Higher fluid intake diluting urine to reduce kidney-stone recurrence is one of the best-supported hydration benefits. Skin and cognition effects are real but smaller/overstated, and 'over-drinking' provides no bonus once you're already hydrated.

blocks.label: See how hydration fits your overall nutrient picture
blocks.body: Hydration is one lever among several — the Nutrients track shows how it sits alongside the minerals and vitamins it works with.

lessons.title: Electrolytes deep dive
lessons.summary: What sodium, potassium, magnesium, and chloride each do — and when a supplement actually earns its place.

blocks.body:
Lesson 3 introduced the four key electrolytes. This is the deep dive: what each one does, how they balance against each other, and — the question worth real money — **when supplementing helps versus when food already has you covered.**

The short version: for most people eating normal meals, food covers electrolytes automatically. Supplements earn their place in a handful of specific situations, which we'll name precisely.

blocks.title: The four electrolytes, in depth

nodes.label: Sodium (Na⁺)
nodes.detail: The master regulator of **extracellular fluid** and blood volume. Drives nerve impulses and muscle contraction. Lost heavily in sweat. Most people get *plenty* from processed food — the supplement case is the opposite of most nutrients: you add sodium around **heavy sweat, fasting, keto, or fluid-losing illness**, not for daily diet.

nodes.label: Potassium (K⁺)
nodes.detail: The dominant **intracellular** electrolyte; balances sodium and supports healthy blood pressure. Found in fruit, vegetables, legumes, potatoes, dairy. Most people get **too little** — but the fix is food, not pills (high-dose potassium supplements are tightly regulated because excess is dangerous for the heart).

nodes.label: Magnesium (Mg²⁺)
nodes.detail: Cofactor for 300+ enzymes, including the **sodium-potassium pumps** that maintain every gradient. Involved in muscle relaxation, nerve function, and sleep. Commonly under-consumed; among the more defensible electrolyte supplements when diet is short — glycinate/citrate forms are well-absorbed.

nodes.label: Chloride (Cl⁻)
nodes.detail: Sodium's partner anion — together they carry most extracellular charge and maintain acid-base balance. Also a building block of **stomach acid**. You almost never need to think about it separately: where there's dietary sodium (salt = sodium chloride), there's chloride.

blocks.title: How the electrolytes balance each other
blocks.simple: Sodium pulls water out of cells; potassium and the pumps that move them pull it back in. Health comes from the *ratio* and the constant pumping, not from any one mineral alone.
blocks.mechanism: Sodium is concentrated outside cells, potassium inside — a gradient maintained by the **sodium-potassium ATPase pump**, which uses energy (and magnesium as a cofactor) to push 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. This gradient powers nerve signals, muscle contraction, and nutrient transport. Chloride follows sodium to keep charge neutral; magnesium keeps the pumps and hundreds of other enzymes running. Disturb one and the others shift — e.g. low magnesium impairs the pump, which can worsen potassium loss.
blocks.studies: Population evidence consistently links **higher potassium and lower sodium intakes** (i.e. a better Na:K ratio, the pattern of whole-food diets like DASH) with healthier blood pressure. Magnesium intake below recommendations is common in modern diets, and correcting a genuine shortfall supports normal muscle and nerve function and may aid sleep quality in those who are low. Crucially, these are about **balance and adequacy** — there's no benefit to loading electrolytes beyond need, and excess sodium or supplemental potassium carries real risk.

blocks.title: When supplementing actually helps
blocks.body: **Add electrolytes when:** you're sweating heavily (long/hot exercise, manual labor), **fasting** or on a strict **keto/very-low-carb** diet (low insulin makes kidneys dump sodium), recovering from **illness with vomiting or diarrhea**, or eating a very clean whole-food diet so low in salt that you feel light-headed/headachy on hot days. **You probably don't need them when:** you eat normal meals with some salt and produce, and you're not doing prolonged hard exercise — food has it covered.

blocks.title: Choosing and using electrolytes sensibly
items: Match the situation: sodium is the one you replace around sweat/fasting/illness — not a daily habit for most.
Favor **potassium and magnesium from food** (produce, legumes, nuts, dairy); use supplements to close a measured gap, not as routine.
Skip the sugar if you don't need fuel — many sports drinks are mostly sugar; plain electrolyte mixes exist.
If you take blood-pressure, heart, or kidney medication, check with a clinician before adding sodium or potassium.

blocks.question: For someone on a strict keto or fasting protocol, which electrolyte most often needs deliberate replacing?
options: Chloride — it's the first to run out
Sodium — low insulin makes the kidneys excrete more of it
None — fasting raises all electrolytes
Only magnesium, never sodium
blocks.explanation: Low carbohydrate intake lowers insulin, which signals the kidneys to excrete more sodium (and water with it). That's why 'keto flu' and fasting fatigue often respond to added sodium — plus magnesium and potassium. With normal eating, food covers these automatically.

blocks.body: ⚕️ Potassium and sodium both have meaningful upper limits and interact with common medications and kidney/heart conditions. Use supplements to fill a real gap in the situations above — not 'just in case' — and get personalized advice if you have a relevant condition.

blocks.label: Check your mineral coverage
blocks.body: See where your potassium, magnesium, and sodium intake actually land before deciding whether a supplement is worth it.

supplements.title: Supplements
supplements.intro: A supplement should earn its place — close a real gap in your diet, in a form your body can use, at a dose that actually does something, backed by evidence and made by someone who tests it. This track teaches you to judge any product on those terms instead of on the label's promises.

lessons.title: What a supplement actually is
lessons.summary: Supplementing a gap, not replacing food — and the regulatory reality that makes quality your job.

blocks.body:
The word gives it away: a supplement is meant to **supplement** a diet, not stand in for one. Whole food delivers nutrients bundled with fiber, healthy fats, and thousands of cooperating compounds your body evolved alongside. A capsule delivers an isolated dose. Both can be useful — but they're not interchangeable.

The right mental model is simple: find a **specific gap** (a nutrient you genuinely fall short on, a goal food can't easily reach), then fill that gap with the cleanest, best-dosed product you can find. A supplement with no gap to fill is just expensive urine.

blocks.title: Gap first, product second
blocks.body: Before buying anything, ask: what gap does this fill, and how would I know it's filled? If you can't answer, you don't need the product yet. The strongest cases are real shortfalls — vitamin D in low-sun climates, B12 on a vegan diet, omega-3 if you eat little fish, magnesium for most modern diets.

blocks.heading: The regulatory reality (read this twice)
blocks.body:
Here's what surprises most people: in the US, dietary supplements are **not pre-approved** by the FDA the way drugs are. A company does not have to prove a supplement works, or even that the bottle contains what the label claims, **before** selling it. The FDA can act only **after** a product is on the market and shown to be unsafe or misbranded.

That means quality varies wildly between brands — and verifying it falls on you. The good news: a few simple checks (covered in this track) separate the trustworthy products from the rest.

⚕️ This track is education, not medical advice. Supplements can interact with medications and conditions, and 'natural' does not mean 'safe.' Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting anything new — especially if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, taking prescription medication, or managing a health condition.

blocks.question: What is the single best reason to take a given supplement?
options: An influencer or ad recommended it
It fills a specific, identifiable gap in your diet or needs
It's popular and lots of people take it
It can't hurt, so why not
blocks.explanation: A supplement earns its place by closing a real gap. 'It can't hurt' is false for several nutrients (fat-soluble vitamins and minerals have real upper limits), and popularity is not evidence. Start from your actual needs, not the marketing.

blocks.title: Your routine

blocks.label: Browse supplements scored on evidence and quality
blocks.body: Formulate grades products on form, dose, evidence, and testing — so you can spot the ones that actually earn their place.

lessons.title: Form & bioavailability — half the game
lessons.summary: The same nutrient in different chemical forms can absorb wildly differently.

blocks.body:
Two bottles can both say "magnesium 200 mg" and deliver completely different results. What matters isn't just how much is in the pill — it's how much your body can actually **absorb and use**. That's **bioavailability**, and it's governed largely by the chemical *form* the nutrient comes in.

Form is roughly half the game. A premium, well-absorbed form at a fair dose beats a cheap, poorly-absorbed form every time — even at the same number on the label.

blocks.prompt: Magnesium oxide is the cheapest, most common magnesium form on shelves. Roughly what fraction of it does the body actually absorb?
blocks.explanation: Magnesium oxide is poorly soluble and absorbed at only a few percent — often cited around 4%. So a 400 mg oxide pill may deliver less usable magnesium than a smaller dose of a chelated form like **magnesium glycinate** or **citrate**, which absorb far better and are gentler on the gut. The label number is meaningless without the form.

blocks.title: Form changes everything — four classic examples

nodes.label: Magnesium: glycinate/citrate vs oxide
nodes.detail: Oxide is cheap but barely absorbed (~4%) and tends to cause loose stools. Chelated forms (glycinate, citrate, malate, threonate) absorb much better and are better tolerated. Glycinate is calming and gentle; citrate is a solid all-rounder.

nodes.label: Folate & B12: methylated vs synthetic
nodes.detail: Many people carry MTHFR gene variants that reduce conversion of synthetic folic acid into the active form. Methylfolate (5-MTHF) and methyl-/adenosyl-B12 are pre-activated, so they work regardless. Worth choosing if B-vitamins are your goal.

nodes.label: Minerals: chelated vs cheap salts
nodes.detail: Chelated minerals (bound to amino acids — e.g. zinc bisglycinate, iron bisglycinate) generally absorb better and irritate the gut less than oxides, carbonates, and sulfates. The chelate 'escorts' the mineral across the gut wall.

nodes.label: Curcumin: needs a delivery boost
nodes.detail: Plain turmeric curcumin is absorbed terribly on its own. Adding black-pepper extract (piperine) can raise its bioavailability dramatically; specialized formulations (phytosome, nanoparticle) do similar. A curcumin product with no absorption enhancer is mostly wasted.

blocks.title: Why form decides absorption
blocks.simple: The same nutrient can come bound to different molecules. Some of those packages dissolve and cross your gut wall easily; others mostly pass straight through. Choosing the right form is how you make the dose count.
blocks.mechanism: Absorption depends on solubility, the molecular 'carrier' a nutrient is bound to, and how it interacts with gut transporters and stomach acid. Chelation binds a mineral to amino acids, keeping it soluble and shuttling it across the intestinal lining via peptide pathways instead of competing in the harsher mineral-ion route. For curcumin, piperine slows the liver and gut enzymes (glucuronidation) that would otherwise clear it before it reaches the blood. For folate, the methylated form bypasses the MTHFR enzyme step some people can't perform efficiently.
blocks.studies: Comparative absorption studies consistently rank organic/chelated mineral forms above inorganic oxides and carbonates, and show large bioavailability gains for curcumin when paired with piperine or formulated as a phytosome. The MTHFR-and-folate story is well-established in nutritional genetics, though for most people ordinary folate status is fine; the methylated form is a sensible default rather than a proven necessity for everyone. The headline lesson is robust: form materially changes how much nutrient reaches your bloodstream.

blocks.body: Quick rule of thumb: prefer chelated minerals (names ending in -glycinate, -citrate, -malate, -bisglycinate), methylated B-vitamins, and curcumin with an absorption enhancer. Avoid oxide and carbonate mineral forms unless price is the only concern.

blocks.label: Look up a nutrient's best forms
blocks.body: The ingredient encyclopedia breaks down forms and bioavailability for common supplements, so you can choose the version that actually absorbs.

lessons.title: Dose — what you actually take per day
lessons.summary: RDA vs clinical dose vs fairy dust — and why more isn't always better.

blocks.body:
The number that matters is the dose you genuinely take **per day** — which means **serving size × servings per day**, not the biggest figure on the front of the bottle. A label that boasts a big amount "per 3 capsules" is telling you a different story than it first appears.

Three dose concepts are worth keeping straight:
- **RDA** (Recommended Dietary Allowance): the amount that prevents deficiency in most people. A floor, not an optimum.
- **Clinical / therapeutic dose**: the amount actually used in the studies that showed a benefit. This is usually what you want for an effect.
- **Fairy dust**: a token, sub-effective amount sprinkled in so an ingredient can appear on the label — common in 'proprietary blends.'

blocks.title: Beware the proprietary blend
blocks.body: When a label lists a 'proprietary blend' with one combined weight instead of the dose of each ingredient, you can't tell whether the active ingredients are at clinical levels or fairy-dust traces. Prefer products that disclose each ingredient's exact dose.

blocks.prompt: Creatine monohydrate is one of the most-studied supplements there is. What's the standard daily maintenance dose used in most research?
blocks.explanation: The well-established maintenance dose is about **5 g per day** (some protocols front-load with ~20 g/day split into doses for a week first). A product giving you 1 g 'creatine complex' is under-dosed versus the evidence. Knowing the studied dose lets you check whether a product delivers it.

blocks.question: A bottle's front says '1000 mg' but the supplement facts say 'serving size: 3 capsules.' You take 1 capsule a day. What's your actual daily dose?
options: About 333 mg
Impossible to know
blocks.explanation: The 1000 mg is per 3-capsule serving, so one capsule is about 333 mg. Always read the serving size and divide. Front-label numbers are marketing; the supplement facts panel is the truth.

blocks.body: ⚕️ More is not always better. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate in the body and can become toxic at high doses, and minerals like iron, zinc, and selenium have real upper limits. Don't 'mega-dose' to be safe — respect tolerable upper intake levels and check with a clinician before going above standard amounts.

blocks.label: Check the real per-day dose on any product
blocks.body: Formulate scores dose against the clinically studied range, so under-dosed and proprietary-blend products are easy to spot.

lessons.title: Evidence — how to weigh a claim
lessons.summary: Mechanism vs RCT vs meta-analysis, and what makes a study trustworthy.

blocks.body:
Every supplement comes with claims. Learning to grade them — to tell 'plausible idea' from 'proven in humans' — is the most powerful skill in this whole track, because it lets you ignore most of the noise.

The key distinction: a **mechanism** (a reason something *might* work) is not the same as **evidence** that it actually does in real people. Plenty of ideas that look beautiful on paper, or work in a petri dish or in mice, fall apart in human trials.

blocks.label: The number of participants in a single landmark supplement RCT (the VITAL trial of vitamin D and omega-3) — the scale needed to settle a question one small study or a mechanism never can.

blocks.title: The evidence ladder — from weakest to strongest

nodes.label: Mechanism / theory
nodes.detail: A plausible biological reason it could work. Necessary but weak on its own — most mechanisms never pan out in practice. Treat 'supports X pathway' as a hypothesis, not a result.

nodes.label: Test-tube & animal studies
nodes.detail: Effects in cells or mice. Useful for discovery, but the doses are often absurd relative to a human, and biology differs. 'Cured cancer in a dish' is the classic overhyped headline. Promising, not proof.

nodes.label: Observational human studies
nodes.detail: Tracks groups of people over time. Can reveal associations but can't prove cause — people who take a supplement often differ in many other ways (the 'healthy-user' effect).

nodes.label: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
nodes.detail: The gold standard: people randomly assigned to supplement or placebo, ideally double-blind. Randomization cancels out confounders, so a difference can be attributed to the supplement itself.

nodes.label: Meta-analyses & systematic reviews
nodes.detail: Pool many RCTs to see the overall picture and whether results replicate. The strongest single source — but only as good as the trials inside it.

blocks.title: What makes an individual study strong
blocks.simple: Trust a study more when it's big, randomized, blinded, uses a real dose for long enough, isn't funded by someone selling the product, and has been repeated by other teams.
blocks.mechanism: Randomization balances unknown confounders across groups so the only systematic difference is the treatment. Blinding (ideally double-blind, where neither participant nor researcher knows who got what) prevents the placebo effect and unconscious bias from creeping in. Adequate sample size gives the statistical power to detect a real effect and reduces false positives. A dose and duration matching real-world use ensures the result is actually relevant. Independent funding and pre-registration reduce the chance results were cherry-picked.
blocks.studies: A useful real example of evidence done well is the VITAL trial — a large, randomized, placebo-controlled study of vitamin D and omega-3 in tens of thousands of adults. It's a model for how a definitive supplement question gets answered, and its nuanced results (benefits for some endpoints, not others) show why a single mechanism or small study is never enough. The broader lesson: weigh the *body* of evidence and its quality, not the loudest single claim. Where high-quality replicated RCTs exist, lean on them; where only mechanism or mouse data exist, stay skeptical.

blocks.question: A supplement ad cites a study showing its ingredient 'killed cancer cells in the lab.' How much should that move you?
options: A lot — that's strong proof it works
A little — it's an early signal that may or may not hold up in humans
Not at all — lab studies are worthless
It depends only on how big the effect was
blocks.explanation: Cell and animal results are how research starts, not how it ends. Many compounds that destroy cells in a dish do nothing useful (or are harmful) at realistic human doses. It's a hint to investigate, never a reason to buy. Demand human RCTs for human claims.

blocks.body: Watch the funding and the verb. Industry-funded studies aren't automatically wrong, but they tilt positive — weigh them with extra caution. And note vague verbs like 'supports,' 'promotes,' or 'helps maintain': those are legally permitted structure/function claims that require far less proof than a direct 'treats' or 'cures' claim.

blocks.label: See the evidence grade behind a supplement
blocks.body: Each ingredient in the encyclopedia carries an evidence summary, so you can judge the strength of a claim before you spend anything.

lessons.title: Quality, testing & stacking
lessons.summary: Third-party seals, certificates of analysis, and how supplements interact with each other and your meds.

blocks.body: Because supplements aren't pre-approved for purity (Lesson 1), a real risk is that the bottle doesn't contain what the label says — or contains things it shouldn't. Independent testing exists precisely to close that gap. Once you trust *what's in the bottle*, the final layer is making the products work **together** instead of against each other.

blocks.prompt: In independent testing of supplements pulled from store shelves, roughly what share fail to match their label (wrong dose, missing active, or contamination) in a typical problem category?
blocks.explanation: It varies a lot by category and brand, but independent labs routinely find that a meaningful fraction — often around a fifth, and far higher in problem categories like some herbals and sports products — don't match their labels or carry contaminants. This is exactly why third-party testing matters: it's your only real guarantee of what's in the bottle.

blocks.title: Third-party testing — the seals worth knowing

nodes.label: NSF Certified
nodes.detail: Independent testing that the product contains what the label says and is free of unsafe contaminants. NSF Certified for Sport additionally screens for banned substances — the standard for athletes.

nodes.label: Informed Sport / Informed Choice
nodes.detail: Batch-level testing specifically for substances banned in competition. Look for it on protein and sports supplements if you're tested.

nodes.label: USP Verified
nodes.detail: United States Pharmacopeia verifies identity, potency, purity, and that the product dissolves properly. A strong general-quality mark.

nodes.label: COA (Certificate of Analysis)
nodes.detail: A lab report for a specific batch showing what was tested and the results. The best brands publish COAs (ideally from an independent lab) so you can verify potency and purity yourself.

blocks.title: Synergy and competition are real
blocks.body: Some nutrients work better together; others fight for the same absorption pathways. The classics: **vitamin D + K2 + magnesium** cooperate in directing calcium where it belongs; **calcium competes with iron and zinc** for absorption (so don't take them at the same time); large doses of one mineral can crowd out another. Timing and pairing matter.

blocks.title: Build a stack that actually works together
items: Take iron away from calcium, coffee, and tea — they sharply reduce iron absorption. Pair iron with vitamin C instead.
Take fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and omega-3s with a meal that has some fat.
Pair vitamin D with K2 and magnesium rather than mega-dosing D alone.
Split competing minerals (calcium vs iron/zinc) into different meals or times of day.
Look for a third-party seal (NSF, USP, Informed Sport) or a published COA before buying.
Re-check your whole stack for overlaps — multiple products can stack the same nutrient past its upper limit.

blocks.body: ⚕️ Supplements can interact with prescription medications — sometimes seriously. A few well-known examples: vitamin K affects blood thinners like warfarin; St. John's Wort weakens many drugs including some antidepressants and birth control; high-dose fish oil and vitamin E can add to bleeding risk. This is not a complete list. Before adding any supplement, tell your doctor or pharmacist everything you take so they can check for interactions — especially if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or on medication.

blocks.label: Audit your stack for overlaps and interactions
blocks.body: Your stack view shows everything together, so you can catch doubled-up nutrients and timing conflicts before they cost you.

lessons.title: Timing & absorption — when you take it matters
lessons.summary: With or without food, fat-soluble with fat, spacing minerals, AM vs PM, and splitting doses.

blocks.body:
You already know form and dose decide how much nutrient reaches your blood (Lessons 2 and 3). **Timing** is the quieter third lever — *when* and *with what* you swallow a supplement can change how much you actually absorb, and how well you tolerate it.

Most timing rules come down to three forces: whether a nutrient needs **fat or stomach acid** to absorb, whether it **competes** with another nutrient for the same doorway into the body, and whether it **nudges you toward energy or calm** at the wrong time of day.

blocks.title: What "take with food" really changes
blocks.body: "With food" is doing two jobs. First, **fat-soluble** nutrients (vitamins A, D, E, K and omega-3s) need dietary fat present to be absorbed properly — a glass of water won't cut it. Second, food **buffers the gut**: minerals like iron, zinc, and magnesium can cause nausea or cramping on an empty stomach, so a meal smooths that out (at the cost of a little absorption for iron specifically).

blocks.title: Timing rules that actually move the needle

nodes.label: Fat-soluble vitamins + omega-3 → with a fatty meal
nodes.detail: Vitamins A, D, E, K and fish oil absorb far better alongside dietary fat. Taking vitamin D with your largest, fat-containing meal can meaningfully raise blood levels versus taking it on an empty stomach. Fish oil with food also cuts the fishy burps.

nodes.label: Iron → empty stomach + vitamin C, away from calcium/coffee/tea
nodes.detail: Iron absorbs best on an empty stomach, and vitamin C boosts it; but calcium, coffee, tea, and whole grains sharply block it. If iron upsets your stomach, take it with a little food — just not a calcium-rich or caffeinated one.

nodes.label: Calcium → split into ~500 mg doses, away from iron/zinc
nodes.detail: The gut can only absorb so much calcium at once, so doses above ~500 mg are wasteful — split them across the day. Keep calcium separate from iron and zinc, which it competes with for absorption.

nodes.label: Magnesium → flexible, often calming in the evening
nodes.detail: Magnesium absorbs fine any time and is gentle taken with food. Many people prefer it in the evening because forms like glycinate feel relaxing and may support sleep — but morning is fine too.

blocks.prompt: Roughly how much elemental calcium can the gut absorb efficiently from a single dose before the rest is largely wasted?
blocks.explanation: Calcium absorption is saturable — efficiency drops sharply above about **500 mg** of elemental calcium in one sitting. So a single 1000 mg tablet delivers less usable calcium than two 500 mg doses taken at different meals. This is the clearest case where *splitting* a dose beats taking it all at once.

blocks.title: AM vs PM, and why splitting doses helps
blocks.simple: Some supplements lean stimulating (B-vitamins, some adaptogens, anything with caffeine) and belong in the morning; others lean calming (magnesium glycinate, often) and suit the evening. And for several nutrients, two smaller doses absorb better than one big one.
blocks.mechanism: Absorption of water-soluble nutrients is often capacity-limited: transporters in the gut wall can only carry so many molecules per unit time, so a large bolus overwhelms them and the surplus passes through (or, for things like vitamin C, gets excreted in urine). Splitting keeps each dose under that ceiling. Time-of-day effects are partly about alertness — B-vitamins participate in energy metabolism and can feel activating, so an evening dose may disturb some people's sleep — and partly about goal: magnesium and certain botanicals are taken at night for their calming, sleep-supportive feel. Spacing competing minerals (calcium vs iron/zinc) into separate meals avoids them fighting over shared transporters.
blocks.studies: The saturable nature of calcium absorption and the iron-blocking effect of calcium, coffee, tea, and phytates are well established in nutrition research and underpin standard clinical advice to split calcium and separate iron from those inhibitors. The benefit of taking vitamin D with a fat-containing meal has been shown in controlled comparisons of fasting versus with-meal dosing. Time-of-day claims (e.g. magnesium for sleep) are more modest — supported by mechanism and some trials but individual, so treat AM/PM placement as optimization, not a hard rule.

blocks.title: Your timing cheat sheet
items: Vitamin D, fish oil, and A/E/K: take with your fattiest meal of the day.
Iron: empty stomach with vitamin C if tolerated; never with calcium, coffee, or tea.
Calcium: cap each dose around 500 mg and split across meals; keep away from iron and zinc.
B-vitamins and stimulating actives: morning, so they don't disturb sleep.
Magnesium: any time, often calming in the evening; fine with food.
When in doubt, taking it consistently every day beats perfect timing — the dose you actually remember wins.

blocks.question: You take 5000 IU of vitamin D each morning with just black coffee, on an empty stomach. What's the easy fix?
options: Switch to a bigger dose to compensate
Take it with a meal that contains some fat
Take it at night instead
Nothing — vitamin D absorbs fine without food
blocks.explanation: Vitamin D is fat-soluble, so it absorbs much better with dietary fat than with coffee alone. Moving it to a meal that has some fat (eggs, avocado, oily fish, nuts) raises how much actually reaches your blood — no dose increase needed.

blocks.label: Set timing on each item in your stack
blocks.body: Your stack lets you schedule items to morning or evening slots, so you can separate competing minerals and put calming supplements at night.

lessons.title: The evidence-backed core
lessons.summary: The short list with genuinely strong human evidence — creatine, omega-3, vitamin D, magnesium, protein, fiber.

blocks.body:
Thousands of products exist; only a handful are backed by strong, replicated human evidence for clear benefits. If you do nothing else with this track, learn this short list — it covers most of what's genuinely worth considering.

Notice what these have in common: they're cheap, well-studied for decades, address common real gaps, and make modest, honest claims. None of them are exciting marketing stories. That's exactly why they're trustworthy.

blocks.label: Published human studies on creatine monohydrate — one of the most thoroughly researched supplements in existence, and consistently safe in healthy people.
blocks.source: Body of creatine research (decades of human trials)

blocks.title: The core six — what each does, who benefits, real dose

nodes.label: Creatine monohydrate — ~3–5 g/day
nodes.detail: Strongest evidence for strength, power, and training performance, with growing research on cognition and aging. Plain monohydrate is the studied, cheap, effective form — fancier versions add cost, not proven benefit. Helps anyone training; vegetarians (who eat less dietary creatine) may notice more.

nodes.label: Omega-3 (EPA + DHA) — ~1–2 g combined/day
nodes.detail: From fish oil or algae. Can help lower high triglycerides and is important if you rarely eat oily fish. Look at the actual EPA+DHA numbers, not the total fish-oil weight. Most benefit goes to people with low fish intake; whole fish is the ideal source.

nodes.label: Vitamin D3 — typically 1000–2000 IU/day (test first)
nodes.detail: A genuine deficiency is common in people with little sun exposure, darker skin, or northern latitudes. Correcting a real deficiency matters; dosing above your needs doesn't add benefit. Ideally guided by a blood test. Pairs well with K2 and magnesium.

nodes.label: Magnesium — ~200–400 mg elemental/day
nodes.detail: Many diets fall short. Involved in hundreds of enzyme reactions; supports normal muscle, nerve, and sleep function. Glycinate and citrate absorb well and are gentle (oxide is poorly absorbed — see Lesson 2).

nodes.label: Protein powder — to fill a daily protein gap
nodes.detail: Not magic — just convenient, concentrated protein (whey, casein, or plant blends). Useful if you struggle to hit your protein target from food, especially when building muscle or aging. Whole-food protein first; powder is the gap-filler.

nodes.label: Fiber — work toward ~25–38 g/day total
nodes.detail: Most people eat far too little. Supports digestion, blood sugar, cholesterol, and the gut microbiome. Food fiber (beans, oats, vegetables, fruit) is best; a psyllium or similar supplement helps close the gap if your diet can't.

blocks.title: Why these earned the 'core' label
blocks.simple: Each of the core six addresses a common real-world gap, has been tested in many human trials (not just mechanism or mice), shows a consistent modest benefit, and is safe at sensible doses. They clear the bar from Lesson 4: human RCTs and meta-analyses, repeated by different teams.
blocks.mechanism: Creatine increases muscle phosphocreatine stores, giving you more rapid energy (ATP) for short, intense efforts — and the brain uses the same energy system. EPA and DHA are structural fats incorporated into cell membranes and are precursors to anti-inflammatory signaling molecules. Vitamin D acts like a hormone, binding receptors throughout the body to regulate calcium, bone, and immune function. Magnesium is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes, including those that make and use ATP. Protein supplies the amino acids that build and repair muscle and most body tissue. Soluble fiber forms gels that slow glucose absorption and bind cholesterol; fermentable fiber feeds beneficial gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids.
blocks.studies: Creatine has one of the deepest evidence bases of any supplement — large bodies of RCTs and meta-analyses support its performance benefits and long-term safety in healthy people. Omega-3 and vitamin D were tested at scale in the VITAL trial (tens of thousands of adults), which showed a nuanced picture: real benefits for some endpoints, not a cure-all — a model of honest, large-scale evidence. Magnesium adequacy and fiber intake are tied to better metabolic and cardiovascular markers across many studies, with the strongest case for people who are genuinely low. Protein needs above the bare-minimum RDA for active and older adults are well supported. The throughline: these aren't hyped — they're the unglamorous, replicated basics.

blocks.body: "Evidence-backed" doesn't mean "everyone needs it." These earn a place only when they fill a gap you actually have — low fish intake, a tested vitamin D deficiency, a protein shortfall, a fiber-poor diet. A supplement that corrects nothing changes nothing. Lesson 9 covers who actually needs what.

blocks.question: A creatine product is marketed as a special 'creatine HCl complex' at 750 mg per serving, costing three times more than plain monohydrate. What's the catch?
options: Nothing — newer forms are always better
It's both under-dosed versus the studied ~3–5 g and pays a premium for a form without proven extra benefit
Creatine HCl is dangerous
You should take five servings to reach the dose
blocks.explanation: Plain creatine monohydrate at ~3–5 g/day is the form the evidence is built on — cheap and effective. Boutique forms charge more without proven superiority, and 750 mg is well under the studied maintenance dose. Match the studied form and dose, and don't overpay for novelty.

blocks.label: Find a well-dosed core supplement
blocks.body: Filter the catalog for these core ingredients and check that dose and form match the evidence before you buy.

lessons.title: Botanicals & adaptogens — promising vs proven
lessons.summary: Ashwagandha, rhodiola, curcumin, ginseng: how they're studied, why the extract matters, and realistic expectations.

blocks.body:
Botanicals are plant-derived supplements; **adaptogens** are a popular subset claimed to help the body resist stress. Some have genuinely encouraging human data — but the category is also where hype, weak studies, and quality problems run highest.

The honest summary: a few botanicals are *promising* with real (if modest and short-term) trials behind them; most are *under-studied*; and almost all are vulnerable to a quality issue you can't see — the wrong plant part, the wrong extract strength, or outright adulteration.

blocks.title: The extract is the active dose
blocks.body: A botanical's effect depends on its **standardized extract** — the concentration of the active compounds, not just the milligrams of powder. "500 mg ashwagandha" tells you little; "600 mg KSM-66 (standardized to ~5% withanolides)" tells you what was actually studied. When a label names no standardization, you can't tell if it matches the research dose or is essentially flavored filler.

blocks.title: Four common botanicals — what the evidence says

nodes.label: Ashwagandha — promising for stress
nodes.detail: Among the better-studied adaptogens. Several short human trials suggest it may modestly reduce perceived stress and support sleep. Look for a standardized extract (e.g. KSM-66 or Sensoril) at the studied dose. Evidence is encouraging but mostly small, short trials — real but not iron-clad.

nodes.label: Rhodiola rosea — promising for fatigue
nodes.detail: Some trials suggest it may ease mental fatigue and improve a sense of stress resilience. Quality is a major issue — rhodiola is frequently adulterated with cheaper species. Standardization to rosavins and salidroside is the marker to look for. Modest, mixed evidence.

nodes.label: Curcumin (turmeric) — promising for inflammation, absorption-limited
nodes.detail: Curcumin has anti-inflammatory signals in trials, but it's absorbed terribly on its own (Lesson 2). It only counts when paired with an absorption enhancer (piperine, phytosome, etc.). Promising for joint comfort; not a proven cure for anything.

nodes.label: Ginseng — mixed, claim-dependent
nodes.detail: Panax (Asian) and American ginseng have a long traditional history and scattered trials for energy, cognition, and immune support, but results are inconsistent and quality varies widely. Treat broad 'energy and vitality' claims with caution.

blocks.title: How botanicals are studied — and why to stay measured
blocks.simple: Most botanical trials are small, short, and use a specific branded extract at a specific dose. That means a positive result applies to *that* extract — not necessarily to the random powder in a cheaper bottle. Promising is not the same as proven, and 'natural' is not the same as 'safe' or 'effective.'
blocks.mechanism: Plants contain dozens of compounds, and only some are active — so the extraction method, plant part, and standardization determine the real dose of what matters. Adaptogens are proposed to act on the body's stress-response system (the HPA axis and stress hormones like cortisol), nudging it toward balance rather than forcing a single direction; curcumin is thought to dampen inflammatory signaling pathways. These mechanisms are plausible, which is exactly why Lesson 4's caution applies: a good mechanism is a hypothesis, not a result.
blocks.studies: Ashwagandha has the most supportive human data of the common adaptogens — multiple small randomized trials suggesting reduced perceived stress — but trials are generally short, modest in size, and often industry-linked, so the effect size and durability are uncertain. Rhodiola and ginseng have more mixed, lower-quality evidence and serious adulteration problems documented by independent testing. Curcumin's anti-inflammatory effects appear in trials but hinge entirely on a bioavailability-enhanced formulation. The fair stance across the category: a few are reasonable to try for the specific, modest claim they were studied for, with a standardized extract from a tested brand — and clear expectations.

blocks.body: ⚕️ "Herbal" and "natural" do not mean harmless. Botanicals can interact with medications and aren't suited to everyone — St. John's Wort, for example, weakens many prescription drugs (covered in Lesson 10). Some are not recommended in pregnancy. Before trying any botanical, especially if you take medication or are pregnant or breastfeeding, check with a doctor or pharmacist.

blocks.question: Two ashwagandha products: A says '450 mg ashwagandha root powder'; B says '600 mg KSM-66 ashwagandha, standardized to 5% withanolides.' Which better matches the research?
options: A — fewer additives means purer
B — it names a standardized extract at a studied dose
They're identical; the words don't matter
Neither can be judged from the label
blocks.explanation: The trials behind ashwagandha used standardized extracts at defined doses, so product B — naming the extract and its withanolide standardization — is the one you can actually compare to the evidence. Plain 'root powder' with no standardization could deliver far less active compound.

blocks.label: Check a botanical's evidence and standardization
blocks.body: The ingredient encyclopedia summarizes the evidence strength and the forms/extracts worth looking for on each botanical.

lessons.title: Who actually needs what
lessons.summary: Life stages, diets, athletes, and tested deficiencies — 'food first, then supplement the gap.'

blocks.body:
There is no universal supplement everyone should take. The right stack is **personal** — it depends on your diet, life stage, health, and any tested deficiencies. The most powerful question isn't "what's the best supplement?" but "what gap do *I* actually have?"

The guiding principle for this whole track: **food first, then supplement the gap.** Whole food delivers nutrients in forms and combinations supplements can't fully copy. Supplements are for the gaps food genuinely can't close for *you*.

blocks.title: Food first, supplement the gap
blocks.body: Reach for a supplement only when there's a real, identified shortfall — a diet that excludes a nutrient (e.g. no animal foods → no B12), a life stage with higher needs (pregnancy → folate), low sun exposure (vitamin D), or a blood test showing a deficiency. A supplement filling no gap does nothing but cost money and risk over-supplementing.

blocks.title: Common gaps by situation

nodes.label: Vegan / vegetarian
nodes.detail: Vitamin B12 is the non-negotiable one — it's essentially absent from plant foods, so supplementation is genuinely necessary on a vegan diet. Often also worth attention: omega-3 (algae-based EPA/DHA), iron, zinc, iodine, and vitamin D. Calcium and protein need planning but are usually achievable from food.

nodes.label: Pregnancy & trying to conceive
nodes.detail: Folate (folic acid) before and during early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural-tube defects and is a standard recommendation. Iron, iodine, choline, and omega-3 (DHA) often matter too, and a prenatal is commonly advised. This is the clearest case to follow clinical guidance, not self-experiment.

nodes.label: Older adults
nodes.detail: B12 absorption declines with age (and with some medications), vitamin D is commonly low, and protein needs are higher to fight muscle loss. Calcium and vitamin D support bone health. Appetite and absorption both tend to fall, widening the gaps food can leave.

nodes.label: Athletes & heavy trainers
nodes.detail: Higher protein needs, plus the strongest case for creatine. Electrolytes and iron (especially in endurance athletes and menstruating women) can matter. Most 'sports' supplements beyond these are marketing — the core basics do the heavy lifting.

nodes.label: Diagnosed deficiencies
nodes.detail: A blood test showing low vitamin D, iron/ferritin, B12, etc. is the gold-standard reason to supplement — you're correcting a measured shortfall, ideally with dosing and follow-up testing guided by a clinician.

blocks.prompt: On a strict vegan diet, how many nutrients are essentially impossible to get from food, so that they genuinely require supplementation?
blocks.explanation: **Vitamin B12** is the one nutrient that is essentially absent from plant foods, so a vegan diet truly requires a B12 supplement (or fortified foods) — a deficiency can cause serious, sometimes irreversible nerve damage. Others (omega-3, iron, zinc, iodine, vitamin D) are worth attention and may need help, but B12 is the non-negotiable.

blocks.title: Why personalization beats a one-size stack
blocks.simple: Your needs are set by what you eat, your age and life stage, your sun exposure, your health conditions, and your blood work. Two people can need completely opposite stacks. Testing where practical, and targeting real gaps, beats copying someone else's routine.
blocks.mechanism: Nutrient requirements shift with physiology. Pregnancy raises demand for folate, iron, and choline to build a new body. Aging reduces stomach acid and intrinsic factor, cutting B12 absorption, and reduces skin's vitamin D synthesis. A vegan diet removes the only reliable dietary B12 source (animal products) and the most bioavailable iron and zinc forms. Intense training increases protein turnover and depletes creatine and electrolytes. Medications can deplete specific nutrients. Because these drivers differ per person, the same supplement can be essential for one individual and pointless for another.
blocks.studies: The strongest, least controversial supplement recommendations are exactly the gap-filling ones: B12 for vegans, folate in early pregnancy (backed by robust evidence for reducing neural-tube defects), vitamin D for the deficient, and protein/creatine for athletes and aging muscle. By contrast, broad multivitamin use in well-nourished people has repeatedly shown little benefit in large trials — reinforcing that supplements pay off when they correct a real deficit, not as blanket insurance. Where a blood test can identify a shortfall, correcting it is the most evidence-based supplementation of all.

blocks.body: ⚕️ This lesson is educational, not medical advice. Pregnancy, nursing, chronic conditions, and any tested deficiency should be managed with a doctor or registered dietitian — including which supplements to take, the dose, and follow-up testing. Don't self-diagnose a deficiency or start high-dose supplements during pregnancy without professional guidance.

blocks.question: Someone eating a varied omnivorous diet with regular sun exposure and good blood work asks which supplements they 'should' take. Best answer?
options: A daily multivitamin, fish oil, and a greens powder for insurance
Possibly none beyond filling any specific gap — food first, supplement only real shortfalls
Whatever is trending right now
The full core six from Lesson 7, regardless of need
blocks.explanation: If the diet is varied, sun exposure is adequate, and labs look fine, there may be no gap to fill — and a supplement that corrects nothing adds nothing. The right move is to identify specific shortfalls (diet, life stage, or test) and target only those. 'Food first, supplement the gap.'

blocks.label: Build a stack around your real gaps
blocks.body: Set your goals and diet, and Formulate highlights the nutrient gaps worth closing — so your stack targets what you actually need.

lessons.title: Safety, interactions & megadosing
lessons.summary: Upper limits, supplement↔medication interactions, fat-soluble accumulation, cycling, and contamination.

blocks.body:
Supplements are widely assumed to be harmless because they're sold without a prescription. They're not. The real risks are concentrated in four areas: taking **too much** of something with an upper limit, **interactions with medications**, the slow **accumulation** of fat-soluble nutrients, and **contamination** in a poorly-made product.

None of this means supplements are dangerous in general — it means a few specific situations demand respect and, often, a conversation with a clinician.

blocks.title: The Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)
blocks.body: Many nutrients have a **UL** — the highest daily amount considered safe for most people. Below it, fine; above it, risk rises. Easy to exceed by accident when several products (a multivitamin + a single nutrient + a fortified food) stack the same nutrient. Total intake from *everything* is what counts against the UL, not any one product.

blocks.title: Where supplements bite — four risk zones

nodes.label: Fat-soluble accumulation (A, D, E, K)
nodes.detail: Unlike water-soluble vitamins (excess flushed out in urine), fat-soluble vitamins are stored in body fat and the liver and build up over time. Chronic high-dose vitamin A or D can become toxic — too much D can raise blood calcium dangerously. More is not safer here.

nodes.label: Mineral overload & competition
nodes.detail: Iron is genuinely toxic in overdose (and a leading cause of poisoning in young children — keep it locked away). High zinc over time can cause copper deficiency. High calcium can crowd out iron and zinc. Minerals have real ceilings.

nodes.label: Supplement ↔ medication interactions
nodes.detail: Some combinations are dangerous: vitamin K vs warfarin (blood thinner); St. John's Wort weakens many drugs (antidepressants, birth control, immunosuppressants, more); high-dose fish oil or vitamin E can add to bleeding risk; some supplements affect how the liver clears medications. Always tell your prescriber what you take.

nodes.label: Contamination & adulteration
nodes.detail: Because purity isn't pre-approved (Lesson 1), some products contain heavy metals, undeclared drugs, or banned substances — most notoriously in some weight-loss, 'sexual enhancement,' and bodybuilding products. Third-party testing (Lesson 5) is your defense.

blocks.title: Megadosing, cycling & tolerance
blocks.simple: Taking far more than the studied dose rarely helps and can hurt — water-soluble surplus is wasted, fat-soluble surplus accumulates, and minerals throw each other off balance. A few supplements may benefit from 'cycling' (periodic breaks), but for most, consistent sensible dosing beats mega-dosing.
blocks.mechanism: Water-soluble vitamins (C, B-complex) are largely excreted once blood levels saturate, so megadoses mostly produce expensive urine — and very high vitamin C can cause GI upset, while certain high-dose B-vitamins have their own toxicities. Fat-soluble vitamins lack this escape valve: stored in tissue, they accumulate toward toxicity. Minerals compete for shared transporters, so overloading one (zinc) induces deficiency in another (copper). 'Cycling' is sometimes proposed to prevent receptor downregulation or tolerance with stimulant-like compounds (e.g. caffeine), where the body adapts and the effect fades — a real phenomenon for caffeine, more speculative for most supplements. The safe default is the studied dose, taken consistently.
blocks.studies: The cautionary evidence here is strong and sometimes sobering: large trials of high-dose beta-carotene found *increased* lung-cancer risk in smokers, and several high-dose antioxidant and vitamin E trials showed no benefit or modest harm — direct evidence that 'more antioxidants = better health' is false. Tolerable upper limits are set by expert bodies from documented toxicity. Supplement-drug interactions like warfarin–vitamin K and St. John's Wort's drug-clearing effects are well-documented in pharmacology. The consistent lesson: respect the studied dose and the UL; bigger is a risk, not a bonus.

blocks.body: ⚕️ This is not medical advice and not a complete interaction list. Supplements can interact seriously with prescription medications and aren't safe for everyone. Before starting, stopping, or mega-dosing any supplement — and especially if you take medication, have a health condition, or are pregnant or breastfeeding — give your doctor or pharmacist a full list of everything you take so they can check for interactions and safe limits.

blocks.question: You already take a multivitamin (100% DV of most nutrients), a separate high-dose vitamin D, and eat fortified cereal and a fortified plant milk. What's the overlooked risk?
options: Nothing — you can't overdose from food and supplements combined
Stacking the same fat-soluble vitamins from multiple sources can push total intake past the safe upper limit
The multivitamin cancels out the cereal
Fortified foods don't count toward your intake
blocks.explanation: Upper limits apply to your *total* intake from all sources combined — supplements plus fortified foods. Several products each contributing the same fat-soluble nutrient (like D or A) can quietly add up past the UL. Audit everything together and don't double up by accident.

blocks.label: Check your stack for doubled-up nutrients
blocks.body: Your stack view totals nutrients across every product, so you can spot overlaps that push you toward an upper limit before they become a problem.

lessons.title: Reading a label & spotting junk
lessons.summary: Proprietary blends, fairy dusting, fillers, % daily value, third-party seals, and marketing red flags.

blocks.body:
This lesson pulls the whole track together into a practical skill: picking up any bottle and judging it in under a minute. The **front** of the label is marketing; the **Supplement Facts panel** on the back is the truth. Learn to read the panel, ignore the front, and most junk products give themselves away instantly.

You already have the pieces — form (L2), dose (L3), evidence (L4), testing (L5). This is how to apply them at the shelf.

blocks.title: Anatomy of the Supplement Facts panel

nodes.label: Serving size & servings per container
nodes.detail: Everything else is 'per serving.' If serving size is 3 capsules and you take 1, you get a third of the listed amounts (Lesson 3). Also tells you how long a bottle really lasts — a 'great deal' with a tiny serving may be costlier per day.

nodes.label: Each ingredient + its exact amount
nodes.detail: Good labels list every active ingredient with its specific dose and form (e.g. 'Magnesium glycinate 200 mg'). This is what lets you check dose against the evidence. A panel that hides individual doses is hiding something.

nodes.label: % Daily Value (%DV)
nodes.detail: How much of the official daily reference a serving provides. Useful for vitamins and minerals to gauge whether a dose is trivial or substantial — but %DV is a deficiency-prevention floor, not an optimal dose, and many ingredients (botanicals, creatine) have no %DV at all.

nodes.label: 'Other ingredients' (the fillers)
nodes.detail: Binders, flow agents, capsule material, sweeteners, colors. A few are normal and harmless; a long list of dyes, fillers, and sweeteners on a simple product is a quality red flag. This is also where allergens and additives you may avoid show up.

blocks.title: Proprietary blends hide fairy dusting
blocks.body: A **proprietary blend** lists several ingredients under one combined weight instead of disclosing each dose. That single number can't tell you whether the good ingredients are at clinical levels or **fairy-dusted** — present in token amounts just to appear on the label (often by listing the cheap, heavy ingredient first and the expensive active last). When you can't see each dose, assume the worst and choose a fully-disclosed product instead.

blocks.prompt: A '1,500 mg Energy & Focus Blend' lists, in order: rice flour, caffeine, taurine, and a trendy adaptogen. The expensive adaptogen is listed last. Roughly how much of that 1,500 mg is likely the adaptogen?
blocks.answerLabel: Likely a tiny fraction — fairy dust
blocks.explanation: Ingredients are listed by weight, high to low. With cheap rice flour and caffeine first and the costly adaptogen last in an undisclosed blend, the adaptogen is almost certainly a token amount — far below any studied dose. The blend exists to *list* the trendy ingredient, not to deliver it. This is fairy dusting in plain sight.

blocks.title: 60-second junk detector
items: Flip to the Supplement Facts panel — judge the back, not the front.
Are individual ingredient doses disclosed? A 'proprietary blend' with one combined weight is a red flag.
Do the key doses match the studied amounts (Lessons 3 & 7)? Under-dosed = fairy dust.
Are the forms good (chelated minerals, methylated B's, standardized extracts)? (Lessons 2 & 8.)
Is there a third-party seal (NSF, USP, Informed Sport) or a published COA? (Lesson 5.)
Is 'Other ingredients' short and clean, or a wall of dyes, fillers, and sweeteners?
Be wary of marketing red flags: 'miracle,' 'detox,' 'clinically proven' with no citation, '#1 doctor recommended,' celebrity endorsements, before/after photos, and proprietary 'secret' formulas.

blocks.body: Marketing tell: vague structure/function verbs ('supports,' 'promotes,' 'helps maintain') are legally easy to claim and require little proof (Lesson 4). Sweeping cure language ('treats,' 'cures,' 'reverses') on a supplement is either illegal or a lie — both are reasons to put the bottle down.
