blocks.question: Two pre-workouts. A discloses every ingredient and dose, has an NSF seal, and a short filler list. B has a '6,000 mg proprietary blend,' a celebrity endorsement, and 'clinically proven' with no study cited. Which is the better buy?
options: B — the bigger blend number means more actives
A — full dose disclosure, third-party tested, clean label
Whichever is cheaper per serving
Can't tell without trying both
blocks.explanation: Product A lets you verify exactly what you're getting, is independently tested, and isn't hiding behind a blend or unsupported claims. Product B's big blend number is meaningless without per-ingredient doses, and 'clinically proven' with no citation plus a celebrity is pure marketing. Transparency and testing win.

blocks.label: Compare products on dose, form, and testing
blocks.body: Formulate scores every product on dose, form, evidence, and quality — so the proprietary-blend and fairy-dusted ones are easy to spot and skip.

nutrition.title: Nutrition & Macros
nutrition.intro: Strip away the diet wars and nutrition comes down to two questions: how much energy you take in, and what that energy is made of. This track gives you a working model of calories and the three macronutrients — protein, carbs, and fat — with real, defensible targets you can actually use.

lessons.title: Energy balance — the calorie equation
lessons.summary: What a calorie is, where your daily burn comes from, and why counting is an estimate.

blocks.body:
A **calorie** (technically a kilocalorie) is just a unit of energy. Eat more energy than you spend and your body stores the surplus, mostly as fat; eat less and it draws on reserves. That balance — energy in versus energy out — is what ultimately governs body weight.

But "weight" and "health" aren't the same thing. Calories decide the *direction* of the scale; the *quality* of those calories decides how you feel, perform, and age. You can lose weight on junk and gain it on whole food. This track holds both ideas at once.

blocks.title: Calories govern weight, quality governs health
blocks.body: Energy balance sets whether you gain, hold, or lose. Food quality and macro composition set your body composition, energy, hunger, and long-term health. Optimise both — they answer different questions.

blocks.title: Where your daily burn (TDEE) comes from
blocks.simple: Your total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) is everything you burn in a day. It's mostly just being alive, plus a chunk for moving, plus a small cost for digesting food.
blocks.mechanism: TDEE = BMR + activity + the thermic effect of food (TEF). **BMR** (basal metabolic rate) is the energy to keep you alive at rest — heart, brain, kidneys, cell maintenance — and is typically 60–70% of TDEE. **Activity** splits into deliberate exercise plus NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis: fidgeting, walking, standing) and varies enormously between people. **TEF** is the energy spent digesting and processing food, roughly 10% of intake — but it's not flat across macros: protein costs ~20–30% of its own calories to process, carbs ~5–10%, fat ~0–3%.
blocks.studies: BMR is estimated with equations like Mifflin-St Jeor from height, weight, age, and sex, then multiplied by an activity factor (~1.2 sedentary to ~1.9 very active). These predictions carry real error — individuals can differ from the estimate by 10–20% — so any calculated number is a starting hypothesis, not a fact. NEAT in particular varies several hundred calories per day between people and adapts when you over- or under-eat, which is part of why the body resists simple energy manipulation.

blocks.prompt: How many calories does one gram of FAT provide?
blocks.explanation: Fat packs **9 kcal per gram** — more than double protein and carbohydrate, which each provide about **4 kcal/g**. (Alcohol sits in between at ~7 kcal/g.) This energy density is why a splash of oil or a handful of nuts adds up fast, and why fat is a useful lever for hitting — or trimming — a calorie target.

blocks.body: Calorie counting is an **estimate stacked on estimates**: food labels have a legal margin of error, your absorption isn't 100%, and your real TDEE is a prediction. Treat the number as a dial to adjust by results — not a precise ledger. If the scale isn't moving as expected over 2–3 weeks, change the input, not your faith in the math.

blocks.question: Which is the LARGEST component of most people's daily calorie burn?
options: Deliberate exercise
The thermic effect of food
BMR — the cost of just staying alive at rest
Digestion of protein
blocks.explanation: BMR is typically 60–70% of total daily expenditure. Exercise is usually a smaller, more variable slice than people assume — which is why you can't reliably out-train a poor diet, and why what you eat matters more than most workout plans admit.

blocks.label: See your macro and calorie totals
blocks.body: Formulate estimates your targets and shows today's intake against them — the fastest way to turn the calorie equation from theory into a habit.

lessons.title: Protein — the macro most people under-eat
lessons.summary: What protein does, the real per-bodyweight target, quality, and meal timing.

blocks.body: Protein is the structural and functional macro. It's not just for muscle — it's the raw material for enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and the constant repair of every tissue. Of the three macros, it's also the most **satiating** (keeps you full) and the most metabolically expensive to process. For most people, getting *enough* protein is the single highest-leverage diet change available.

blocks.title: What protein actually does

nodes.label: Muscle protein synthesis
nodes.detail: Dietary protein supplies amino acids to build and repair muscle. This is how you preserve (or grow) lean mass — critical for strength, metabolism, and staying mobile as you age. The amino acid leucine is the key trigger that switches synthesis on.

nodes.label: Satiety & body composition
nodes.detail: Protein blunts hunger more than carbs or fat per calorie, and its high thermic effect (~20–30% of its calories spent digesting it) means a chunk is 'lost' to processing. Both make adequate protein a powerful tool for fat loss without misery.

nodes.label: Enzymes & immune function
nodes.detail: Nearly every reaction in the body is catalysed by an enzyme — all proteins. Antibodies that fight infection are proteins too. Under-eating protein quietly degrades repair, immunity, and recovery.

nodes.label: Structure everywhere
nodes.detail: Collagen in skin, tendons, and bone; keratin in hair and nails; transport proteins in blood. Protein is the body's building material, turned over continuously and needing daily resupply.

blocks.prompt: How much PROTEIN per day should an active 70 kg / 154 lb adult aim for?
blocks.explanation: A solid default for an active adult is about **1.6 g per kg of body weight** — for 70 kg that's ~112 g/day. The useful range runs from ~1.2 g/kg (lightly active) up to ~2.0 g/kg (hard training or a fat-loss phase, where extra protein protects muscle). Note this is far above the RDA of 0.8 g/kg, which is a floor to prevent deficiency — not an optimum for an active person.

blocks.title: Protein quality: complete, leucine, and DIAAS
blocks.simple: Not all protein is equal. 'Complete' proteins (animal foods, soy) have all the amino acids you need in good proportion. Plant proteins are often lower in one or two — easily fixed by eating a variety.
blocks.mechanism: Your body needs nine **essential amino acids** it can't make itself. A 'complete' protein supplies all nine in roughly the ratios you need. The amino acid **leucine** is the specific trigger for muscle protein synthesis — you want roughly 2.5–3 g of leucine in a meal to maximally switch synthesis on, which is why per-meal protein amount (not just daily total) matters. Plant proteins tend to be lower in leucine and one limiting amino acid (e.g. lysine in grains, methionine in legumes), so combining sources covers the gaps.
blocks.studies: Protein quality is increasingly scored by **DIAAS** (Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score), which improves on the older PDCAAS by measuring true digestibility at the end of the small intestine. By DIAAS, animal proteins and soy/whey score highest (often >1.0), while most single plant proteins score lower — but a varied plant-based diet with adequate total protein readily meets needs. The practical takeaway: if you eat mostly plants, aim a little higher on total protein and spread sources, and consider that whole-day amino acid balance matters more than any single meal.

blocks.title: Spread it across the day
blocks.body: Muscle protein synthesis responds to a per-meal dose, and there's a ceiling per sitting (~0.4 g/kg, often ~25–40 g). So 3–4 protein-anchored meals beat cramming your whole target into dinner. Distribution is the detail most people miss after they fix total intake.

blocks.title: Your protein target

blocks.label: Log a meal and watch your protein total
blocks.body: Build your diet in the app and see whether you're actually hitting your protein target — most people are surprised how far under they start.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates — fuel, not the enemy
lessons.summary: What carbs are for, fiber vs sugar, glycemic response, and how much you need.

blocks.body: Carbohydrates are your body's preferred fast fuel — especially for the brain and for high-intensity effort. They've been demonised by diet culture, but the real story is about *which* carbs. The gap between a bowl of lentils and a can of soda is enormous, even though both are 'carbs.'

blocks.label: The brain's roughly fixed daily glucose demand. Your body can make glucose from protein and fat when needed, but carbs are the direct, efficient supply — and the dominant fuel for hard, anaerobic exercise.

blocks.title: Fiber vs sugar, and the glycemic response
blocks.simple: All carbs are chains of sugar, but how fast they hit your blood varies wildly. Fiber doesn't digest into sugar at all — it slows everything down and feeds your gut. Refined sugar hits fast and hard.
blocks.mechanism: Digestible carbs break down to glucose, raising blood sugar and triggering insulin to shuttle it into cells. The **glycemic response** — how high and fast blood sugar rises — depends on the food's structure, fiber, fat, and protein content, and how processed it is. **Fiber** is carbohydrate your enzymes can't break down: soluble fiber forms a gel that slows glucose absorption and lowers cholesterol; insoluble fiber adds bulk and speeds transit. Crucially, fiber is fermented by gut bacteria into short-chain fatty acids that nourish the colon lining and influence metabolism and inflammation.
blocks.studies: Large prospective cohorts consistently link higher fiber intake — especially from whole grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables — with lower cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and all-cause mortality. The evidence for fiber is among the most robust in nutrition. Conversely, high intake of added sugars and refined carbs (especially sugar-sweetened drinks) tracks with worse metabolic outcomes. The signal isn't 'carbs bad' — it's 'refined and stripped, bad; whole and fiber-rich, good.'

blocks.prompt: How much FIBER should an adult aim for per day?
blocks.explanation: Recommended fiber is roughly **25 g/day for women and 38 g/day for men** (or ~14 g per 1000 kcal). Most people in Western countries get barely half that — around 15 g. Closing that gap, by leaning on whole grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables, is one of the most evidence-backed dietary upgrades you can make.

blocks.title: Carbs aren't the enemy — refined carbs are the problem
blocks.body: Your carb *need* scales with activity: an endurance athlete genuinely needs a lot; a sedentary person needs far less. But for everyone, the priority is the same — get carbs from whole, fiber-rich sources and minimise refined sugar and white starch. Quality first, then quantity to match your activity.

blocks.question: Two foods have the same total carbohydrate. Which most reliably blunts the blood-sugar spike?
options: The one eaten later in the day
The one higher in fiber, fat, and protein
The one that's a 'natural' sugar like honey
It makes no difference — carbs are carbs
blocks.explanation: Fiber, fat, and protein all slow gastric emptying and glucose absorption, flattening the rise. 'Natural' sugars like honey are still rapidly absorbed sugar. The food's whole context — not its sugar's label — drives the glycemic response.

blocks.label: Compare carb sources in the food reference
blocks.body: Browse foods to see fiber and carb quality side by side — it makes the 'whole vs refined' difference concrete.

lessons.title: Fat — essential, not fattening
lessons.summary: Essential fatty acids, fat-soluble vitamins, fat types, and the omega balance.

blocks.body: Fat carries an unfair reputation — partly because its name matches the tissue we want to lose, and partly from decades of low-fat dogma. But dietary fat is **essential**: some of it your body literally cannot make, and you need it to absorb whole categories of vitamins. Fat is not fattening *per se* — excess total calories are. The real question is which fats, and in what balance.

blocks.title: The roles of dietary fat

nodes.label: Essential fatty acids
nodes.detail: Omega-3 (ALA) and omega-6 (LA) are 'essential' — your body can't synthesise them, so they must come from food. They build cell membranes and are the precursors to signalling molecules that regulate inflammation, clotting, and more.

nodes.label: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption
nodes.detail: Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in fat, not water — you absorb them far better alongside dietary fat. A fat-free salad can leave much of its vitamin content unabsorbed. A little olive oil isn't indulgence; it's chemistry.

nodes.label: Hormones & cell membranes
nodes.detail: Cholesterol and fatty acids are the backbone of cell membranes and the raw material for steroid hormones (including testosterone and estrogen). Chronically very-low-fat diets can blunt hormone production.

nodes.label: Dense, steady energy
nodes.detail: At 9 kcal/g, fat is the most energy-dense macro and a slow-burning fuel. It adds satiety and flavour — useful, but also why it's easy to over-consume calories from.

blocks.title: Fat types and the omega-3:6 balance
blocks.simple: Unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish, avocado) are the ones to build your diet around. Saturated fat is fine in moderation. Trans fats — from old-style partial hydrogenation — are the ones to avoid entirely.
blocks.mechanism: Fats differ by their carbon-chain structure. **Monounsaturated** (one double bond; olive oil, avocados) and **polyunsaturated** (multiple double bonds; fish, seeds, nuts) fats are generally heart-favourable. **Saturated** fats (no double bonds; solid at room temp — butter, fatty meat) raise LDL cholesterol in many people but exist on a spectrum and aren't a simple villain. **Trans** fats, mostly industrial partially-hydrogenated oils, are uniquely harmful — they raise LDL and lower HDL — and are now banned or phased out in many countries. Within polyunsaturates, **omega-3** and **omega-6** compete for the same enzymes; omega-6 derivatives tend to be more pro-inflammatory, omega-3 derivatives (EPA/DHA) more resolving.
blocks.studies: Replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat is one of the better-supported dietary swaps for cardiovascular risk, though the picture is more nuanced than 1980s low-fat advice implied. Omega-3s (EPA/DHA from fatty fish) have reasonable evidence for cardiovascular and triglyceride benefits. The modern Western diet is heavily skewed toward omega-6 (from refined seed oils) relative to omega-3; while the exact 'ideal ratio' is debated, the practical move everyone agrees on is the same — eat more omega-3 (oily fish, walnuts, flax, chia) rather than obsessing over a precise number.

blocks.body: The fat fixes that matter most are simple: **eliminate trans fats**, **favour unsaturated sources** (olive oil, nuts, fish, avocado), and **eat oily fish or another omega-3 source regularly**. Get those right and the finer ratio debates barely move your health needle.

blocks.question: Which fat-related move is most clearly worth doing for nearly everyone?
options: Cutting dietary fat as low as possible
Avoiding trans fats and eating more omega-3 sources
Maximising omega-6 from refined seed oils
Switching entirely to saturated fats
blocks.explanation: Trans fats are uniquely harmful and worth eliminating, and most people are skewed toward omega-6 and short on omega-3. Going very-low-fat risks essential fatty acid intake, fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and hormone production. Moderate, mostly-unsaturated fat is the sweet spot.

blocks.label: Check your fat and omega intake
blocks.body: See your fat breakdown and whether your omega-3 intake is landing where it should — then adjust meals accordingly.

lessons.title: Putting it together — building your plate
lessons.summary: Energy vs nutrient density, fiber's role, setting a macro split, and the one heuristic that works.

blocks.body: You now have the parts. The skill is assembling them into a way of eating you'll actually keep. Two ideas do most of the work: **nutrient density** (nutrition per calorie) and a couple of simple rules that make good choices the default — so you don't have to weigh and calculate forever.

blocks.title: Energy density vs nutrient density
blocks.body: Energy density is calories per bite; nutrient density is nutrition per calorie. Whole foods — vegetables, fruit, legumes, lean protein — tend to be high in nutrients and low in energy density, so you can eat satisfying volumes without overshooting calories. Ultra-processed foods invert this: energy-dense, nutrient-poor, and engineered to be easy to over-eat.

blocks.title: Setting a personal macro split
blocks.simple: Don't start with percentages. Set protein by your body weight first, set fat to a sensible minimum for hormones and vitamins, and let carbs fill the rest based on how active you are.
blocks.mechanism: A robust way to build a split: (1) **Protein** — anchor at ~1.6 g/kg (range 1.2–2.0 depending on activity, age, and goal; older adults need well above the basic RDA, at least ~1.2–1.5 g/kg, to fight age-related muscle loss). (2) **Fat** — set a floor of roughly 0.6–1.0 g/kg (about 20–35% of calories) to cover essential fatty acids, fat-soluble vitamins, and hormones. (3) **Carbs** — fill the remaining calories; scale up if you train hard, down if you're sedentary or in a fat-loss phase. Percent-of-calories splits (e.g. 30/40/30) are fine as a description but a poor starting point, because they don't adapt to your size the way per-kilogram targets do.
blocks.studies: Across controlled trials, when protein and total calories are matched, the exact carb-to-fat ratio has a surprisingly small effect on body composition for most people — which is why 'best diet' debates so often end in a tie. The diet you adhere to wins. That frees you to choose a split based on your activity, your satiety, and what you'll sustain, rather than chasing a magic ratio.

blocks.label: Roughly how much fiber the average Western adult falls short by each day (target ~25–38 g, typical intake ~15 g). Closing this single gap improves satiety, gut health, and long-term disease risk.

blocks.title: Protein first, fiber second
blocks.body: If you remember one rule, make it this. Build each meal around a protein source, then a fiber-rich plant (vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fruit). Do that and protein, satiety, micronutrients, and gut health largely take care of themselves — and the calories tend to self-regulate, because protein and fiber are the two most filling things you can eat.

blocks.title: Your build-a-plate playbook
items: Anchor every meal with a protein source first — aim for a palm-sized-plus portion.
Add a fiber-rich plant second — fill half the plate with vegetables, legumes, fruit, or whole grains.
Choose unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, avocado, fish) and avoid trans fats.
Favour whole over refined: the more processing, the more energy-dense and nutrient-poor it tends to be.
Match carb quantity to your activity — more on hard-training days, less when sedentary.
Don't chase a perfect macro ratio; chase a pattern you'll repeat for years.

blocks.label: Build your diet and check the totals
blocks.body: Put the playbook to work: log a day of meals, then see your protein, fiber, and macro split land against your targets.

lessons.title: Fiber — the forgotten macro
lessons.summary: Soluble vs insoluble, how fiber feeds your gut, satiety and blood sugar, and how to actually hit 25–38 g.

blocks.body:
Fiber is the macronutrient nobody counts. It's technically a carbohydrate, but one your own enzymes can't digest — so it slips past the small intestine largely intact and does its most interesting work in the colon. That "indigestible" quality is exactly why it's so valuable: it slows, bulks, and feeds in ways that pure calories never could.

Most people in Western countries eat barely half of what's recommended. Closing that gap is one of the most evidence-backed, lowest-risk upgrades in all of nutrition — and it costs nothing but a few smarter food swaps.

blocks.title: Soluble vs insoluble — two jobs, one nutrient
blocks.simple: Fiber comes in two broad types. Soluble fiber dissolves into a gel that slows digestion and feeds your gut bacteria. Insoluble fiber doesn't dissolve — it adds bulk and keeps things moving. Most fiber-rich foods carry both.
blocks.mechanism: **Soluble fiber** (oats, beans, apples, psyllium, barley) absorbs water and forms a viscous gel in the gut. That gel slows gastric emptying and glucose absorption, blunting blood-sugar spikes, and it binds bile acids so the liver pulls cholesterol from the blood to replace them — which is how soluble fiber lowers LDL. **Insoluble fiber** (whole-grain bran, vegetable skins, nuts, seeds) passes through largely unchanged, adding stool bulk, drawing water in, and speeding transit — the main lever against constipation. Whole foods deliver a mix, so you rarely need to think about which is which; you just need to eat real plants.
blocks.studies: Large prospective cohorts and meta-analyses consistently link higher fiber intake — especially from whole grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables — with lower rates of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, colorectal cancer, and all-cause mortality. The dose-response is roughly linear across the realistic intake range, and the evidence base is among the most robust in nutrition. Soluble fiber's LDL-lowering and glucose-blunting effects are well demonstrated in controlled trials; insoluble fiber's benefits show up most clearly for digestive regularity and transit.

blocks.title: Fiber feeds the colony you can't see
blocks.body: Your gut hosts trillions of bacteria, and the fermentable (mostly soluble) fiber you eat is their food. They ferment it into short-chain fatty acids — butyrate, propionate, acetate — that nourish the colon lining, help regulate appetite and blood sugar, and influence inflammation. When people say fiber is good for your gut, this is literally what they mean: you're not just feeding yourself, you're feeding the microbes that work for you.

blocks.prompt: How much fiber should an adult man aim for per day?
blocks.explanation: Recommendations land at roughly **38 g/day for men and 25 g/day for women**, or about **14 g per 1000 kcal** — a useful way to scale it to your own intake. Typical Western intake is only ~15 g, so most adults are running at less than half their target. The gap, not the target, is the story: even moving from 15 to 25 g is a meaningful win.

blocks.label: Typical fiber intake for the average Western adult — well under half the ~25–38 g target. Whole grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables are where the missing fiber lives.

blocks.body: Ramp up fiber **gradually** and drink more water as you do. Jumping from 15 g to 40 g overnight invites gas and bloating while your gut bacteria adapt — add ~5 g every few days instead, and the discomfort largely disappears. Fiber needs water to do its bulking and gel-forming job, so hydration and fiber rise together.

blocks.title: Easy ways to add 5–10 g of fiber
items: Swap refined grains for whole: brown rice, whole-grain bread, oats over white versions.
Add a serving of legumes — beans, lentils, chickpeas — to one meal a day (often ~6–8 g per half-cup, ~12–15 g per cooked cup).
Leave skins on fruit and vegetables where edible (apple, potato, pear).
Make a piece of whole fruit or a handful of nuts/seeds your default snack.
Stir a tablespoon of chia, flax, or psyllium into yogurt, oats, or a smoothie.

blocks.question: Which type of fiber is most responsible for lowering LDL cholesterol and blunting blood-sugar spikes?
options: Insoluble fiber, by adding stool bulk
Soluble fiber, by forming a gel and binding bile acids
Neither — fiber has no effect on cholesterol or blood sugar
Both equally, through the same mechanism
blocks.explanation: Soluble fiber forms a viscous gel that slows glucose absorption and binds bile acids, prompting the liver to draw cholesterol from the blood. Insoluble fiber's main job is bulk and transit — important for regularity, but not the LDL/glucose lever.

blocks.label: See your daily fiber against your target
blocks.body: Log a typical day and check where your fiber actually lands — most people are surprised how far short they start, and how a couple of swaps close the gap.

lessons.title: Calorie quality & nutrient density
lessons.summary: Why two identical-calorie diets aren't equal — energy density, nutrient density, protein leverage, and whole vs refined.

blocks.body:
"A calorie is a calorie" is true for the scale and misleading for everything else. Two diets at the same calorie total can leave you full or starving, nourished or deficient, steady or spiking. The energy number governs weight; what that energy is *made of* governs how easy that weight is to maintain and how good you feel doing it.

This lesson is about the difference between those two diets — and the handful of properties that explain it.

blocks.title: Energy density vs nutrient density
blocks.body: **Energy density** is calories per gram of food — how many calories a bite delivers. **Nutrient density** is nutrition (protein, fiber, vitamins, minerals) per calorie. Whole foods like vegetables, fruit, legumes, and lean protein are low in energy density and high in nutrient density — you can eat satisfying volumes without overshooting. Ultra-processed foods invert both: dense in calories, thin on nutrients, and engineered to be easy to over-eat.

blocks.title: Why volume and water make low-energy-density food filling
blocks.simple: Foods full of water and fiber take up space in your stomach for very few calories. Your body senses that volume and stretch, not just calories — so a big bowl of vegetables fills you up far more than the same calories of crackers.
blocks.mechanism: Satiety is driven partly by **gastric distension** (stomach stretch receptors) and partly by hormonal signals released as food moves through the gut. Water and fiber add weight and volume without calories, so a low-energy-density meal physically fills the stomach at a fraction of the energy cost. Protein and fiber also slow gastric emptying and trigger satiety hormones (like GLP-1 and PYY), extending fullness. Refined, dry, fatty foods pack many calories into little volume and clear the stomach fast — so you can eat a lot of energy before your body registers 'full.'
blocks.studies: Controlled feeding studies show that when people are served lower-energy-density meals, they tend to eat a similar *weight* of food but consume fewer calories — and report equal fullness. This is the core finding behind volume-based eating approaches: people eat to a roughly consistent food mass, so reducing calories per gram lets them eat the same amount while taking in less energy. The effect is robust enough that it's a recommended strategy in obesity research, not a fad.

blocks.title: Protein leverage — why low-protein diets drive overeating
blocks.simple: Your appetite seems to prioritise hitting a protein target. If a diet is low in protein, you keep eating — chasing the protein — and overshoot total calories along the way. Hit your protein, and the drive to keep eating eases.
blocks.mechanism: The **protein leverage hypothesis** proposes that humans have a stronger appetite drive for protein than for carbs or fat. If the protein concentration of the diet is diluted (as it is in many ultra-processed foods, which are mostly refined carbs and fat), you must eat more total food — and more total calories — to reach your protein target. Adequate protein both satisfies this drive and is the most satiating macro per calorie, so it does double duty: it stops the chase and fills you up.
blocks.studies: Experimental studies that manipulate dietary protein percentage support the core prediction: lowering protein density tends to increase total energy intake, and raising it tends to lower it, with people passively eating fewer calories on higher-protein diets without trying. The hypothesis is debated as a complete explanation for obesity, but the practical implication — that adequate protein helps regulate overall intake — is well supported and consistent with everything else we know about protein and satiety.

blocks.prompt: Roughly how much THERMIC EFFECT (calories burned digesting it) does protein have, as a percentage of its own calories?
blocks.explanation: Protein costs about **20–30% of its own calories** just to digest and process — far more than carbs (~5–10%) or fat (~0–3%). So even at equal label calories, a high-protein meal nets you fewer usable calories. This is part of why two identical-calorie diets aren't truly identical: the macro mix changes how much energy you actually keep.

blocks.body: "Whole vs refined" isn't moralising — it's mechanics. Refining strips fiber, water, and often micronutrients while concentrating calories, removing exactly the properties (volume, slow digestion, nutrient density) that make food filling and nourishing. The same 200 calories as an apple versus apple juice versus an apple pastry behave completely differently in your body, even though the calorie label may be similar.

blocks.question: Two snacks have the same calories. Which is more likely to keep you full longer for the fewest 'kept' calories?
options: A handful of crackers — dense and quick to eat
A bowl of vegetables and lean protein — high volume, high protein and fiber
A spoon of oil — most energy-dense, so most filling
It makes no difference — calories are calories
blocks.explanation: Volume, water, fiber, and protein all drive fullness and slow digestion, and protein's high thermic effect means a chunk of its calories are 'lost' to processing. For weight, the calorie number rules — but for satiety and how the food behaves, composition matters enormously.

blocks.label: Compare foods by nutrient density
blocks.body: Browse the food reference to see calories alongside protein, fiber, and micronutrients — it makes the energy-density vs nutrient-density difference concrete.

lessons.title: Meal timing & frequency
lessons.summary: Meal-frequency myths, the breakfast question, intermittent fasting evidence, pre/post-workout nutrition, and circadian eating.

blocks.body:
Few areas of nutrition carry more confident folklore than *when* and *how often* to eat. Six small meals to "stoke the metabolism." Never skip breakfast. Don't eat after 8 pm. Most of these claims are far weaker than they sound — and a few have real, if modest, evidence behind them.

The honest summary up front: for body weight, *total intake* dominates timing. But timing can still affect adherence, performance, and — at the margins — metabolic health. Let's separate the signal from the myth.

blocks.title: Meal frequency: does grazing 'boost metabolism'?
blocks.simple: Eating more often doesn't speed up your metabolism. The number of meals barely matters for weight — what matters is the total food across the day. Pick the frequency you'll actually stick to.
blocks.mechanism: The myth comes from the thermic effect of food: each meal costs energy to digest, so people assume more meals means more burning. But TEF scales with *how much* you eat, not how many times — six small meals and three larger meals of the same total food produce roughly the same total TEF. There's no metabolic 'stoking' from frequent eating. What frequency *does* affect is hunger management and protein distribution: spreading protein across 3–4 meals helps maximise muscle protein synthesis, which is a real reason to favor a few protein-anchored meals over one big one.
blocks.studies: Controlled trials and reviews consistently find no meaningful effect of meal frequency on metabolic rate or fat loss once total calories and protein are matched. Studies on very high meal frequencies (6+) show no advantage and sometimes worse appetite control. The practical takeaway: choose a meal pattern based on your appetite, schedule, and ability to hit your protein and calorie targets — not on a metabolism myth.

blocks.title: The breakfast question
blocks.body: "Breakfast is the most important meal" is marketing more than science. Randomised trials show that eating or skipping breakfast, by itself, doesn't reliably cause weight loss or gain — what matters is total daily intake. Some people genuinely perform and eat better with breakfast; others naturally aren't hungry until midday and do fine skipping it. It's a personal-fit question, not a universal rule.

blocks.title: Intermittent fasting — what the evidence actually says
blocks.simple: Intermittent fasting (e.g. eating only within an 8-hour window) is mainly a tool to eat less without counting — by shrinking the eating window, many people naturally cut calories. Most of its benefits trace back to that calorie reduction, not to fasting magic.
blocks.mechanism: Common forms include **time-restricted eating** (a daily window, e.g. 16:8), **alternate-day fasting**, and the **5:2** pattern. Proposed unique mechanisms include lower insulin during the fast, a metabolic switch toward fat-burning, and cellular 'cleanup' (autophagy). These are biologically real, but in humans the dominant practical effect of IF is simply that a compressed window makes it easier to eat fewer total calories. Aligning the eating window earlier in the day may add a small circadian benefit (see below).
blocks.studies: When intermittent fasting is compared head-to-head with standard calorie restriction *at matched calories*, the two produce similar fat loss and metabolic outcomes — strong evidence that calorie control, not fasting per se, drives most results. Some trials suggest modest extra benefits for blood sugar and blood pressure, especially with early time-restricted eating, but findings are mixed and effect sizes small. IF suits people who prefer fewer eating decisions and don't get derailed by hunger; it's a poor fit for those prone to binge after the fast, people with a history of disordered eating, and some athletes. It's a *tool*, not a requirement.

blocks.label: Approximate extra fat loss from intermittent fasting versus standard calorie restriction when total calories are matched — most IF benefits come from eating less, not from the fasting itself.

blocks.title: Nutrition around a workout

nodes.label: The anabolic 'window' is wide
nodes.detail: The idea that you must eat protein within 30 minutes of training is overstated. Muscle stays primed for hours, and total daily protein matters far more than precise timing. The practical advice: have protein in the meals on either side of your workout, and don't stress the stopwatch.

nodes.label: Pre-workout: fuel and comfort
nodes.detail: A meal with carbs and some protein a few hours before training supports performance, especially for longer or harder sessions. If you train fasted and feel fine, that's okay for general fitness — but most people perform better fed.

nodes.label: Post-workout: protein + carbs
nodes.detail: After training, protein supports repair and carbs help replenish muscle glycogen. This matters most if you train hard, twice a day, or fasted. For a single daily session with adequate daily protein, it's a minor optimisation, not a make-or-break.

nodes.label: Total day beats any single moment
nodes.detail: Hitting your daily protein and calorie targets reliably outranks any workout-timing trick. Get the day right first; fine-tune timing only after the fundamentals are locked in.

blocks.title: Circadian eating
blocks.body: Your metabolism isn't identical around the clock. Insulin sensitivity and the thermic effect of food tend to be higher earlier in the day, and in some studies large late-night meals are linked to worse metabolic markers, though that link is weaker. The conservative, evidence-aligned move: weight your intake toward earlier in the day where it fits your life, and avoid making your biggest meal a late-night one — but don't treat a clock as a hard rule.

blocks.question: What does the strongest evidence say drives the results people get from intermittent fasting?
options: A unique fat-burning effect that calorie restriction can't replicate
Mostly the reduction in total calories that a shorter eating window produces
Speeding up the metabolism by skipping meals
Forcing the body into ketosis every day
blocks.explanation: When calories are matched, intermittent fasting and standard calorie restriction produce similar results — so most of IF's benefit comes from making it easier to eat less, not from the fast itself. It's a useful tool for some people, not a metabolic shortcut.

blocks.label: Plan your meals around your day
blocks.body: Build a meal pattern that fits your schedule and hits your protein target — the timing details matter far less than landing your daily totals.

lessons.title: Hunger, satiety & why diets fail
lessons.summary: Ghrelin and leptin, protein/fiber/volume for fullness, sleep and stress on appetite, the set-point debate, and sustainable deficits.

blocks.body:
Most diets don't fail because the math was wrong. They fail because hunger, biology, and life wear down willpower until the plan collapses. Understanding *why* you get hungry — and how to eat in a way that keeps hunger manageable — is more useful than any specific diet.

This lesson is about the appetite system: the hormones that run it, the foods that quiet it, the lifestyle factors that hijack it, and how to set a deficit you can actually live with.

blocks.title: Ghrelin and leptin — the hunger thermostat
blocks.simple: Two main hormones tune your appetite. Ghrelin is the 'I'm hungry' signal from your stomach; it rises before meals and falls after. Leptin is the 'I have enough energy' signal from your fat tissue; more body fat normally means more leptin and less hunger.
blocks.mechanism: **Ghrelin** is secreted by the stomach, peaks before meals, and drops after eating — it's a short-term hunger driver. **Leptin** is produced by fat cells in proportion to fat mass; it acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and signal energy sufficiency over the longer term. The catch: when you lose weight, leptin falls (less fat = less signal) and ghrelin tends to rise, so your brain reads the deficit as a threat and ramps up hunger while quietly lowering energy expenditure. This adaptive response is a major reason weight loss gets harder over time and regain is so common. In obesity, the brain often becomes resistant to leptin's signal, so high leptin no longer suppresses appetite well.
blocks.studies: Studies tracking people through weight loss document measurable rises in ghrelin and drops in leptin and energy expenditure that persist for months — the body actively defends against the loss. This is the physiological backbone of the 'set-point' idea and explains why maintenance, not the loss itself, is the hard part. It also reframes dieting failure as a biological headwind to manage, not a simple lack of discipline.

blocks.title: Protein, fiber, and volume — the satiety trio
blocks.body: The three most filling properties of food are **protein** (most satiating macro per calorie, plus high thermic effect), **fiber** (slows digestion, adds bulk, feeds gut hormones), and **volume/water** (physically fills the stomach for few calories). Build meals around these and you can eat in a calorie deficit while feeling fed — the single most important practical skill for making a diet survivable.

blocks.title: Lifestyle factors that hijack appetite

nodes.label: Sleep deprivation
nodes.detail: Short sleep raises ghrelin and lowers leptin, increases cravings for high-calorie food, and weakens impulse control. People consistently eat more — especially junk — when underslept. Fixing sleep is an underrated appetite intervention.

nodes.label: Chronic stress
nodes.detail: Stress elevates cortisol, which can increase appetite and drive cravings for calorie-dense 'comfort' foods. Emotional eating short-circuits the normal hunger signals entirely — you eat to soothe, not to fuel.

nodes.label: Ultra-processed food
nodes.detail: Engineered combinations of sugar, fat, salt, and soft texture are easy to over-eat and weakly satiating per calorie. They bypass the body's natural fullness brakes, so you take in more before you feel done.

nodes.label: Liquid calories
nodes.detail: Calories from drinks (soda, juice, alcohol, sweet coffees) barely register on the appetite system — they don't reduce how much you eat at the next meal, so they stack on top of your intake almost invisibly.

blocks.title: The set-point debate
blocks.simple: Your body seems to defend a certain weight range, pulling you back with hunger and a slower metabolism when you drop below it. How fixed that 'set point' really is — and whether you can shift it — is genuinely debated.
blocks.mechanism: The **set-point theory** holds that the body regulates fat mass around a defended range via leptin, ghrelin, and energy-expenditure adjustments — like a thermostat. A competing view, sometimes called the **settling point**, argues that body weight settles wherever your environment, habits, and food supply push it, rather than being defended around a fixed biological target. The truth is likely a blend: there's clear evidence of biological defense (the adaptive hunger and metabolic slowdown of dieting), but the 'set point' is not rigidly fixed — sustained changes in behavior and environment can shift where the body settles over time.
blocks.studies: The adaptive responses to weight loss (rising hunger hormones, falling expenditure) are well documented and real. But the strong claim that weight is locked to an immovable target is not well supported — populations and individuals do shift weight durably with lasting environmental and behavioral change. The practical reading: expect biological resistance to a deficit, plan for it, and favor slow, sustainable change that gives the body time to settle, rather than aggressive cuts that trigger the strongest defenses.

blocks.body: A **moderate, sustainable deficit beats an aggressive one.** A cut of roughly 10–20% below maintenance (often ~300–500 kcal/day) tends to be large enough to lose fat steadily but small enough to keep hunger, energy, training, and adherence intact. Crash deficits trigger the strongest hormonal pushback and are the ones people abandon. Slow and survivable wins the long game.

blocks.question: Why does losing weight tend to get harder the longer a diet goes on?
options: Calories stop counting once you've lost some weight
Falling leptin and rising ghrelin increase hunger while energy expenditure drops — the body defends against the loss
Your metabolism speeds up uncontrollably
Protein stops being filling after a few weeks
blocks.explanation: As you lose fat, leptin falls and ghrelin rises, raising hunger, while NEAT and metabolic rate decline. The body actively resists the deficit. Knowing this lets you plan around it — moderate deficits, high protein and fiber, good sleep — instead of blaming willpower.

blocks.label: Build meals that keep you full
blocks.body: Anchor your day with protein, fiber, and high-volume foods, then check the totals — the easiest way to eat in a deficit without feeling starved.

lessons.title: Sugar, alcohol, caffeine & sweeteners
lessons.summary: Added vs intrinsic sugar, alcohol's calories and metabolism, caffeine, and what the evidence says about non-nutritive sweeteners.

blocks.body: Sugar, alcohol, caffeine, and artificial sweeteners are the most argued-about items in the diet conversation — and the most surrounded by hype in both directions. Here's a calm, evidence-based pass at each: what's genuinely worth limiting, what's overblown, and what the data honestly can't yet say.

blocks.title: Added vs intrinsic sugar
blocks.body: The sugar in a soda and the sugar in an apple are chemically similar but nutritionally worlds apart. **Intrinsic sugar** comes packaged inside whole foods with fiber, water, and nutrients that slow its absorption — that's why whole fruit is fine. **Added sugar** is sugar put into foods during processing, stripped of that context, delivering rapid calories with little else. Health guidance targets *added* sugar (commonly suggesting under ~10% of calories, or less), not the sugar naturally in fruit and dairy.

blocks.title: Alcohol — the 'fourth macro' your body prioritises
blocks.simple: Alcohol provides 7 calories per gram — almost as much as fat — and your body treats it as a toxin to clear first. While it's metabolising alcohol, fat-burning is paused, which is part of why drinking can stall fat loss beyond just the calories.
blocks.mechanism: Ethanol yields about **7 kcal/g**, sitting between carbs/protein (4) and fat (9). The body has no way to store alcohol, so the liver prioritises clearing it — oxidising ethanol to acetaldehyde and then acetate, which is burned for energy. While this is happening, the oxidation of fat (and to a degree carbs) is suppressed, so the calories you eat alongside drinks are more likely to be stored. Add that drinks are easy, liquid, non-filling calories, and that alcohol disinhibits eating, and the impact on a fat-loss effort can exceed the raw calorie count.
blocks.studies: The old notion of a clear 'J-shaped curve' where moderate drinking protects the heart has weakened substantially as studies controlled better for confounders; current consensus leans toward 'less is better,' with no intake established as risk-free, and clear dose-dependent increases in several cancers and other harms at higher intakes. For body composition, alcohol's calories count and its metabolic priority blunts fat oxidation. None of this requires total abstinence for everyone — but it does mean alcohol is a cost to spend deliberately, not a free pass.

blocks.prompt: How many calories does one gram of ALCOHOL provide?
blocks.explanation: Alcohol delivers **7 kcal per gram** — closer to fat (9) than to protein or carbs (4 each). And unlike those macros, it can't be stored, so the body burns it preferentially and pauses fat oxidation while it does. That's why drinks are an easy, often-overlooked source of calories that can quietly derail a deficit.

blocks.title: Caffeine — a genuinely useful tool, with caveats
blocks.simple: Caffeine reliably improves alertness, mood, and exercise performance, and is one of the few supplements with strong evidence. The main caveats are sleep (it lingers for hours), tolerance (effects fade with daily use), and individual sensitivity.
blocks.mechanism: Caffeine blocks **adenosine receptors** — adenosine is the molecule that builds up through the day and makes you sleepy — so caffeine masks fatigue rather than removing the underlying need for rest. It also modestly raises adrenaline. Its half-life is roughly 5 hours but varies widely by genetics, so an afternoon coffee can still impair night-time sleep. Regular use builds tolerance to some effects (especially alertness), and abrupt cessation causes withdrawal headaches.
blocks.studies: Caffeine is one of the best-evidenced performance aids: meta-analyses show small but consistent improvements in endurance, power, and perceived exertion, typically at ~3–6 mg/kg before exercise. Moderate habitual intake (commonly cited as up to ~400 mg/day for most adults) appears safe for the general population and is associated in cohort studies with neutral-to-favorable health outcomes. The biggest real-world downside is sleep disruption from drinking it too late — protect sleep by keeping caffeine to the morning and early afternoon.

blocks.title: Non-nutritive sweeteners — what the evidence actually shows
blocks.simple: Artificial and low-calorie sweeteners let you cut sugar calories, and swapping sugary drinks for diet versions helps people reduce intake and lose modest weight. Whether they have downsides of their own is debated, and the evidence is still developing.
blocks.mechanism: Non-nutritive sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, stevia, etc.) taste sweet but provide little or no calories and don't raise blood sugar meaningfully. The open questions are whether they influence appetite, sweet cravings, or the gut microbiome in ways that matter for health — biologically plausible mechanisms that have been proposed but not firmly established in humans.
blocks.studies: Randomised trials generally show that replacing sugary drinks with non-nutritive-sweetened ones leads to lower calorie intake and modest weight loss versus keeping the sugar — a real benefit for people trying to cut added sugar. Major safety reviews have found approved sweeteners safe at typical intakes. However, some observational studies link heavy sweetener use to worse metabolic outcomes (likely confounded — people already at risk often switch to diet products), and some research raises questions about gut-microbiome effects, leaving the long-term picture genuinely unsettled. The defensible position: low-calorie sweeteners are a reasonable tool to reduce sugar, water is still the best default drink, and there's no strong evidence to fear moderate use.

blocks.body: A simple priority order from the evidence: **cut added sugar (especially sugary drinks) first**, **treat alcohol as deliberate calories to spend, not waste**, **use caffeine as a tool but protect your sleep**, and **see low-calorie sweeteners as a reasonable bridge off sugar — not something to fear or to over-rely on.** Water remains the default beverage.

blocks.question: Which statement best reflects the current evidence on alcohol and body composition?
options: Alcohol has no calories, so it can't affect weight
Alcohol provides ~7 kcal/g and its metabolism temporarily suppresses fat-burning
Alcohol speeds up fat loss because the body burns it off instantly
Alcohol counts as a carbohydrate at 4 kcal/g
blocks.explanation: Ethanol yields ~7 kcal/g — between carbs/protein and fat — and the body prioritises clearing it, pausing fat oxidation in the meantime. Combined with its easy, non-filling, disinhibiting nature, that makes alcohol an outsized factor in a fat-loss effort relative to its calorie label.

blocks.label: Track your added-sugar and beverage calories
blocks.body: Log a typical day and see how much of your intake comes from added sugar and drinks — often the easiest calories to trim without feeling deprived.

lessons.title: Eating for your goal
lessons.summary: Fat loss vs maintenance vs muscle gain — calculating a deficit or surplus, recomposition, protein, refeeds, and adjusting over time.

blocks.body:
Everything in this track converges here: turning the principles into a plan aimed at a specific goal. Whether you want to lose fat, hold steady, or build muscle, the structure is the same — set an energy direction, anchor protein, fill the rest with quality food, then adjust based on real-world results.

This lesson walks through each goal, how to set the numbers, and — most importantly — how to keep adjusting as your body responds.

blocks.title: The three goals, side by side

nodes.label: Fat loss — a calorie deficit
nodes.detail: Eat below maintenance so the body draws on fat stores. Keep the deficit moderate (~10–20%, often 300–500 kcal/day), push protein high to protect muscle, and lean on fiber and volume to stay full. Aim for roughly 0.5–1% of body weight lost per week — faster tends to cost muscle and adherence.

nodes.label: Maintenance — energy balance
nodes.detail: Eat at maintenance to hold your weight. Underrated as a goal: maintenance is where you practise the habits that make any future loss or gain stick, and a deliberate maintenance phase after a diet helps the body and appetite hormones recalibrate.

nodes.label: Muscle gain — a calorie surplus
nodes.detail: Eat modestly above maintenance (often ~5–15%, ~150–350 kcal/day) to fuel growth, paired with progressive resistance training and ample protein. A small surplus builds muscle with minimal fat; a large 'dirty bulk' mostly adds fat you'll later have to cut.

blocks.title: Calculating your deficit or surplus
blocks.simple: Estimate your maintenance calories (your TDEE), then subtract for fat loss or add for muscle gain. The estimate is just a starting point — you confirm and adjust it by watching the scale and the mirror over a few weeks.
blocks.mechanism: Start by estimating **maintenance (TDEE)** — either from an equation (BMR via Mifflin-St Jeor × an activity factor) or, more reliably, by tracking your intake at a stable weight for 1–2 weeks. For **fat loss**, subtract ~10–20% (a 70 kg moderately active person at ~2400 kcal might cut to ~1900–2100). For **muscle gain**, add ~5–15% (~150–350 kcal). The classic '~3500 kcal ≈ 1 lb of fat' rule is a rough teaching device, not a precise law — adaptive changes in metabolism and NEAT mean real-world results drift from the arithmetic, which is exactly why you adjust by feedback.
blocks.studies: Predictive equations carry real error (individuals can differ from the estimate by 10–20%), and the body adapts — NEAT and metabolic rate shift in response to over- and under-eating, partially offsetting the change. This is well documented and is why no calculated number should be treated as fixed. The reliable method is empirical: set a starting target, track weight trend over 2–3 weeks, and revise the calories if the trend isn't matching the goal. The math gets you in the ballpark; feedback gets you to the target.

blocks.title: Body recomposition — losing fat and gaining muscle at once
blocks.body: It's possible to gain muscle while losing fat ('recomp'), but it's slow, and it works best for specific groups: beginners to resistance training, people returning after a layoff, and those with higher body fat. The recipe is roughly maintenance calories (or a very small deficit), high protein (~1.6–2.2 g/kg), and consistent progressive strength training. For lean, trained individuals, recomp gets very hard — they generally make faster progress by alternating focused gain and loss phases.

blocks.prompt: For a fat-loss phase, what's a sensible WEEKLY rate of weight loss as a percentage of body weight?
blocks.explanation: Aiming to lose about **0.5–1% of body weight per week** is the sweet spot: fast enough to see steady progress, slow enough to preserve muscle and adherence. For an 80 kg person that's ~0.4–0.8 kg/week. Faster loss increasingly comes from muscle and water, ramps up hunger, and is harder to sustain — patience genuinely pays off in body composition.

blocks.body: **Protein stays high across every goal.** In a deficit it protects muscle from being burned for fuel; in a surplus it supplies the raw material for new muscle; at maintenance it keeps you full and preserves lean mass. Whatever your goal, anchor it first — roughly 1.6 g/kg, trending toward 2.0+ g/kg during a fat-loss phase or hard training — then arrange carbs and fat around it.

blocks.title: Refeeds, diet breaks, and adjusting over time
blocks.simple: Long diets benefit from occasional planned higher-calorie days or weeks. They give your hormones, training, and willpower a breather — and as you lose weight, you'll need to lower calories again because a smaller body burns less.
blocks.mechanism: A **refeed** is a short (1–2 day) planned increase in calories, mostly from carbs, during a longer deficit; a **diet break** is a longer return to maintenance (1–2 weeks). Both aim to ease the adaptive downsides of prolonged dieting — restoring some leptin, replenishing glycogen for training, and relieving the psychological strain. Separately, because your TDEE falls as you lose weight (less mass to maintain, plus adaptive reductions), a deficit that worked at the start eventually becomes maintenance — so you must periodically recalculate and trim again, or increase activity, to keep losing.
blocks.studies: Evidence for structured diet breaks improving fat loss or preserving metabolism is suggestive but mixed — the clearest, most consistent benefit is on adherence and psychological sustainability, which is itself a major determinant of long-term success. Refeeds and breaks aren't mandatory, but they're a sensible tool for longer or more aggressive diets. The non-negotiable principle is feedback-driven adjustment: bodies adapt, so any plan that doesn't get revised over time will eventually stall.

blocks.question: Your weight has stalled three weeks into a fat-loss phase, despite eating the same. What's the most evidence-aligned response?
options: Conclude calories don't matter and give up tracking
Recognise your TDEE has fallen as you lost weight, and modestly cut calories further or add activity
Cut calories drastically all at once to force the scale down
Add a large surplus to 'reset' the metabolism
blocks.explanation: A smaller body burns fewer calories, and dieting brings adaptive reductions in expenditure, so a once-effective deficit becomes the new maintenance. The fix is a modest further cut or more activity — informed by the trend over weeks — not a drastic crash or giving up. Adjust by feedback; that's the whole game.

blocks.label: Set your targets and track toward your goal
blocks.body: Dial in your calorie and macro targets for fat loss, maintenance, or gain, then track the trend over a few weeks and adjust — the feedback loop is what turns a plan into results.

nutrients.title: Vitamins & Minerals
nutrients.intro: Micronutrients are the spark plugs of your metabolism — tiny amounts that decide whether thousands of enzymes fire or stall. This track covers what each one does, who genuinely runs low, how much you actually need (and can overdo), and how to get them from food first.

lessons.title: What micronutrients are — and why 'micro' isn't 'minor'
lessons.summary: Cofactors that make your enzymes work: macro fuel vs micro spark plug.

blocks.body:
Your diet has two layers. **Macronutrients** — protein, carbs, fat — are the fuel and building blocks, measured in grams and hundreds of calories. **Micronutrients** — vitamins and minerals — are measured in milligrams or micrograms and supply zero calories. Yet without them, the fuel can't be burned.

Think of it this way: macros are the gasoline, micros are the spark plug. You can have a full tank and go nowhere if the spark is missing.

blocks.title: Micros are cofactors
blocks.body: Most vitamins and minerals work as **cofactors** — helper molecules an enzyme needs to do its job. Magnesium, zinc, and the B-vitamins each unlock entire families of reactions. Run low and dozens of processes slow at once, which is why deficiency symptoms are so vague and wide-ranging.

blocks.prompt: Magnesium acts as a cofactor for how many distinct enzymatic reactions in the human body?
blocks.explanation: Magnesium is required for **300+** enzymatic reactions — including every step that uses ATP (your energy currency), DNA and protein synthesis, and muscle and nerve function. One mineral, hundreds of jobs. That breadth is exactly why a single shortfall produces such a scattered list of symptoms.

blocks.heading: Vitamins vs minerals
blocks.body:
**Vitamins** are organic molecules (they contain carbon) made by living things — plants, animals, microbes. They're more fragile: heat, light, and air can degrade them.

**Minerals** are inorganic elements that come from soil and water and end up in food. They're indestructible — you can't cook the iron out of spinach — but how well you absorb them varies enormously.

blocks.title: 'Essential' means your body can't make it
blocks.body: An essential nutrient is one you **must** get from food because your body either can't synthesize it at all, or can't make enough. That's the whole reason these show up on labels and RDAs exist — there's no internal backup supply. (Vitamin D and niacin are partial exceptions: your skin makes some D from sunlight, and you make a little niacin from the amino acid tryptophan.)

blocks.question: Why does a single mineral deficiency often cause many unrelated-seeming symptoms?
options: Minerals are stored in fat and leak out slowly
Each micronutrient is a cofactor for many different enzymes at once
The body randomly shuts down organs to conserve energy
Symptoms are mostly psychological
blocks.explanation: Because one micronutrient typically powers dozens or hundreds of reactions across different systems, a shortfall slows all of them simultaneously — producing fatigue, mood changes, poor sleep, cramps, and more, with no single obvious cause.

lessons.title: Fat-soluble vs water-soluble
lessons.summary: Where vitamins are stored, which ones can build up, and timing with food.

blocks.body:
Vitamins split into two camps based on what they dissolve in — and that one property decides how you store them, how you absorb them, and whether you can overdo them.

**Fat-soluble:** A, D, E, K.
**Water-soluble:** the eight B-vitamins and vitamin C.

blocks.title: The two vitamin families

nodes.label: Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K
nodes.detail: Dissolve in fat and are stored in your liver and fatty tissue. Because you bank them, you can go a while without — but you can also build up toxic levels from heavy supplementation. Absorbed best WITH a meal containing some fat. A = vision & immunity, D = bone & immune signaling, E = antioxidant protecting cell membranes, K = blood clotting & directing calcium to bone.

nodes.label: Water-soluble: B-complex + C
nodes.detail: Dissolve in water, are barely stored, and the excess is flushed in urine. So you need a steady, near-daily supply — but toxicity from food is essentially impossible. The B-vitamins run energy metabolism and make red blood cells; vitamin C builds collagen and supports immunity and antioxidant defense.

nodes.label: Storage difference
nodes.detail: Fat-soluble vitamins have a 'tank' (months of D or A can sit in the liver); water-soluble ones have almost no tank, so a gap in intake shows up faster. This is why scurvy (vitamin C) and beriberi (B1) appear within weeks-to-months of a deficient diet.

nodes.label: Toxicity risk
nodes.detail: Toxicity is mostly a fat-soluble concern — A and D in particular, almost always from over-supplementing, never from food. Water-soluble vitamins are far more forgiving, though megadoses of a few (B6, niacin) can still cause problems.

blocks.title: Why fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate
blocks.simple: Fat-soluble vitamins get parked in your liver and fat, so they pile up if you keep taking far more than you use. Water-soluble ones just wash out in urine, so they don't build up the same way.
blocks.mechanism: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed alongside dietary fat (packaged into chylomicrons) and partition into fatty tissue and the liver, which have huge storage capacity and slow turnover. There's no easy excretion route, so chronic excess raises tissue levels. Water-soluble vitamins circulate in blood plasma; once transport proteins and tissue stores saturate, the kidneys filter and excrete the surplus — keeping a tight ceiling.
blocks.studies: The clearest evidence is clinical: vitamin A toxicity (hypervitaminosis A) and vitamin D toxicity (hypercalcemia) are well-documented from high-dose supplements, which is why tolerable Upper Intake Levels exist for them. By contrast, excess vitamin C and most B-vitamins are reliably excreted — large-dose vitamin C studies mostly show extra is simply lost in urine, with GI upset as the main downside, not accumulation.

blocks.body: Take fat-soluble vitamins (and supplements like vitamin D or fish oil) **with a meal that contains some fat** — absorption can be dramatically higher than on an empty stomach. Water-soluble ones (C, B-complex) work fine any time, though some people find B-vitamins energizing and prefer the morning.

blocks.question: Which statement is TRUE about water-soluble vitamins?
options: They're stored in the liver for months
They're the main toxicity risk from food
Excess is largely flushed in urine, so a daily supply matters more
They should always be taken with a fatty meal
blocks.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C) aren't banked in any meaningful way — the surplus is excreted by the kidneys. That makes a steady, near-daily intake important, and makes toxicity from food essentially a non-issue.

lessons.title: The nutrients people actually run low on
lessons.summary: The genuine, common shortfalls — and what deficiency really does.

blocks.body: Most people in wealthy countries get plenty of calories — and still under-consume a short, predictable list of micronutrients. These aren't exotic; they're the everyday gaps that show up again and again in dietary surveys.

blocks.prompt: Roughly what fraction of adults in the US/Europe have vitamin D levels below the commonly recommended sufficiency threshold? (slider = percent)
blocks.explanation: Estimates depend heavily on the cutoff used, the season, latitude, and skin tone — published figures range from roughly a quarter to well over half of adults below sufficiency, with **~40%** a defensible middle estimate for many populations. The point isn't the exact number: vitamin D shortfall is genuinely common, driven by indoor life, sunscreen, higher latitudes, and the fact that very few foods contain meaningful amounts.

blocks.title: The common shortfalls — and what deficiency does

nodes.label: Vitamin D
nodes.detail: Skin makes it from sunlight, but modern indoor life and northern latitudes leave many short. Low D impairs calcium absorption and bone health, and is linked to weaker immune function and low mood. Few foods supply much — fatty fish, egg yolk, fortified dairy.

nodes.label: Magnesium
nodes.detail: A large share of adults fall below the requirement. Refining strips it from grains, and modern diets lean processed. Shortfall shows as muscle cramps, poor sleep, fatigue, and worse stress tolerance. Sources: leafy greens, nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains, dark chocolate.

nodes.label: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)
nodes.detail: The marine omega-3s most people barely eat unless they have oily fish regularly. They're structural fats for brain and eye, and anti-inflammatory. Plant ALA (flax, walnuts) converts to EPA/DHA only poorly. Sources: salmon, sardines, mackerel; algae oil for vegans.

nodes.label: Potassium
nodes.detail: Most people get far less than the target — the flip side of eating too few fruits and vegetables (and too much sodium). Adequate potassium supports healthy blood pressure. Sources: potatoes, beans, leafy greens, bananas, yogurt, tomato.

nodes.label: Fiber
nodes.detail: Technically not a micronutrient, but the single most under-eaten thing on the plate — most adults get about half the target. It feeds gut bacteria, steadies blood sugar, and supports heart health. Sources: legumes, whole grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts.

nodes.label: B12 (cobalamin)
nodes.detail: Found almost only in animal foods, so vegans and vegetarians are at real risk — and absorption drops with age, making older adults vulnerable even on a mixed diet. Deficiency causes fatigue, nerve problems, and a specific anemia. Sources: meat, fish, eggs, dairy; fortified foods or a supplement for plant-based eaters.

nodes.label: Iron
nodes.detail: The most common deficiency worldwide. Menstruating women are especially at risk from monthly losses. Low iron causes fatigue, breathlessness, and poor concentration before it becomes anemia. Sources: red meat, shellfish (heme); beans, lentils, fortified grains, spinach (non-heme).

nodes.label: Calcium, choline, iodine
nodes.detail: Calcium — many fall short, risking weaker bones long-term (dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, tofu). Choline — newly recognized as widely under-consumed; vital for brain and liver (eggs, liver, soy). Iodine — needed for thyroid hormones; intake has slipped as people use less iodized salt and more sea/specialty salts (iodized salt, seafood, dairy).

blocks.label: Of US adults fall short of the magnesium requirement from food alone — one of the most consistently under-consumed minerals.

blocks.body: ⚕️ This is general education, not medical advice. Real deficiency — especially iron, B12, vitamin D, or thyroid-related iodine issues — should be confirmed with a blood test and addressed with a clinician, not self-diagnosed. Symptoms overlap heavily and guessing wrong wastes time.

blocks.title: Your coverage right now

blocks.label: See which nutrients YOUR diet is short on
blocks.body: Formulate rolls up your logged foods and supplements into a coverage view, so you can spot your own gaps instead of guessing from a generic list.

lessons.title: RDA vs optimal vs upper limit
lessons.summary: Why 'enough to avoid disease' isn't the whole story — and why more isn't better.

blocks.body: When you see a "% Daily Value" on a label, that's anchored to the **RDA** (Recommended Dietary Allowance). It's a useful floor — but it answers a narrower question than most people assume.

blocks.title: RDAs prevent deficiency — not necessarily optimize
blocks.body: An RDA is set to meet the needs of ~97–98% of healthy people and **prevent deficiency disease** (scurvy, rickets, anemia). That's not the same as the intake that best supports long-term health or performance. For some nutrients those numbers are close; for others (vitamin D is the classic debate), many researchers argue the optimal range sits above the bare-minimum RDA.

blocks.prompt: What's the adult RDA for vitamin C?
blocks.explanation: The adult RDA for vitamin C is **90 mg/day for men and 75 mg for women** (smokers need ~35 mg more). That's the amount that comfortably prevents scurvy and keeps tissues saturated — reachable from a couple of servings of fruit and vegetables. Megadoses don't raise blood levels much further because absorption is tightly regulated and the excess is excreted.

blocks.title: The U-shaped curve: too little AND too much both harm
blocks.simple: For most nutrients there's a sweet spot. Below it you get deficiency problems; above it, especially with supplements, you can hit toxicity or other harm. More is not automatically better.
blocks.mechanism: Plot health outcome against intake and you often get a U (or J) shape: risk is high at low intake, drops to a broad minimum in the adequate range, then climbs again at very high intake. The rising right-hand arm reflects toxicity (vitamin A, D), pro-oxidant or interfering effects (very high iron, zinc displacing copper), or downstream imbalance. The flat bottom is why 'topping up a gap' helps but 'loading way past your needs' usually doesn't.
blocks.studies: Several large trials cooled early enthusiasm for high-dose single nutrients. Beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in smokers (CARET, ATBC trials). High-dose vitamin E and 'antioxidant cocktail' trials largely failed to show benefit and sometimes hinted at harm. The lesson across this literature: correcting a real deficiency is valuable, but pushing a nutrient far above need in already-replete people rarely helps and can backfire.

blocks.title: The Upper Limit (UL) is the ceiling
blocks.body: The **Tolerable Upper Intake Level** is the most you can take daily with little risk of harm. It mostly matters for supplements (food rarely gets you there). Watch it with vitamin A, vitamin D, iron, zinc, niacin, and B6 — all have documented problems above their ULs. Between the RDA (floor) and the UL (ceiling) is your safe operating range.

blocks.question: Your vitamin C intake already meets the RDA. What does taking a 1,000 mg supplement on top mostly do?
options: Dramatically boosts blood and tissue levels
Is largely excreted — absorption is regulated and tissues are already saturated
Cures the common cold reliably
Builds up to dangerous levels over time
blocks.explanation: Vitamin C absorption is tightly controlled and tissue stores saturate at modest intakes, so most of a megadose is simply excreted. It won't reliably prevent colds, and while it's not stored to toxic levels, very large doses can cause GI upset and, in susceptible people, kidney stones.

lessons.title: Bioavailability & food-first
lessons.summary: Why how much you absorb beats how much you eat — and when a supplement earns its place.

blocks.body: A label tells you how much of a nutrient is *in* a food. **Bioavailability** tells you how much you actually *absorb and use* — and the gap between the two can be huge. The same milligram of iron from steak and from spinach are not equal in your gut.

blocks.title: Heme vs non-heme iron
blocks.simple: Iron from animal foods (heme) is absorbed far more easily than iron from plants (non-heme). So a vegetarian needs more total iron on paper to get the same amount into the body — and the form, not just the number, matters.
blocks.mechanism: Heme iron sits inside a protein ring (from hemoglobin/myoglobin) and is taken up by a dedicated, efficient transporter, fairly insulated from other foods. Non-heme iron must first be reduced from Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and is highly sensitive to its meal context — vitamin C and acids enhance uptake, while phytates (whole grains, legumes), polyphenols (tea, coffee), and calcium suppress it.
blocks.studies: Absorption figures consistently show heme iron absorbed at roughly 15–35% versus non-heme often in the low single digits to ~10%, swinging widely with the meal. This is why iron-deficiency guidance for plant-based eaters emphasizes pairing iron foods with vitamin C and separating them from tea, coffee, and calcium-rich foods.

blocks.title: Absorption helpers and blockers

nodes.label: Vitamin C boosts iron
nodes.detail: Vitamin C reduces non-heme iron to its absorbable form and counters phytates. A squeeze of lemon, bell pepper, or tomato with a bean or lentil meal can multiply iron uptake. Easiest free 'supplement' you have.

nodes.label: Calcium ↔ iron compete
nodes.detail: Calcium and iron share absorption pathways and interfere with each other in the same meal. If you supplement both, take them at different times; if iron is your concern, don't wash an iron-rich meal down with a big glass of milk.

nodes.label: Fat unlocks fat-soluble vitamins
nodes.detail: A, D, E, K and carotenoids need dietary fat to be absorbed well. A salad with a fat-free dressing leaves much of its vitamin A and K behind — add olive oil, avocado, or nuts and absorption jumps.

nodes.label: The food matrix
nodes.detail: Whole foods deliver nutrients packaged with fiber, fats, and other compounds that change how they're absorbed and used — often for the better, and in combinations a single pill can't replicate. Synergy is the rule, not the exception.

blocks.title: Food first — supplements fill gaps
blocks.body: Whole foods come as a matrix: the nutrient plus fiber, fats, phytochemicals, and cofactors that help it work. Isolated high-dose supplements lack that context — which is part of why single-nutrient pills so often underperform the same nutrient from food in trials. Default to food; reach for a supplement to **fill a specific, identified gap**, not to replace eating well.

When a supplement genuinely earns its place: a confirmed deficiency (e.g. iron, B12, vitamin D on a blood test), a nutrient that's hard to get from your diet pattern (B12 and EPA/DHA for vegans, vitamin D in dark winters), or a higher need (pregnancy folate, older adults' B12). Outside those cases, the food version usually wins.

blocks.title: Get more from what you already eat
items: Pair plant iron (beans, lentils, spinach) with a vitamin-C food — lemon, pepper, tomato, citrus.
Keep tea and coffee away from iron-rich meals; they blunt absorption.
Add a little fat to vegetables — olive oil, avocado, nuts — to unlock A, E, K and carotenoids.
Take calcium and iron supplements at different times, not together.
Build meals around whole foods first; treat supplements as targeted gap-fillers, ideally guided by a test.
Take vitamin D and fish oil with your largest, fattiest meal of the day.

blocks.label: Find the best food sources for any nutrient
blocks.body: Browse which foods deliver the most of each nutrient — and lean on food first before deciding whether a supplement is worth it.

lessons.title: Vitamin D — the sunshine hormone you're probably low on
lessons.summary: Why D is the most common shortfall, D3 vs D2, the K2 + magnesium team, and how to test it.

blocks.body:
Vitamin D is barely a "vitamin" at all — it behaves like a hormone. Your skin makes it when UVB sunlight hits cholesterol in the skin, your liver and kidneys then convert it into the active form, and that active form switches genes on and off in nearly every tissue you have.

It's the single most common micronutrient shortfall in the modern world, for one simple reason: we evolved outdoors and now live indoors.

blocks.prompt: Roughly what fraction of adults are below the commonly used vitamin D sufficiency threshold (~30 ng/mL / 75 nmol/L)?
blocks.answerLabel: ~40% (estimates vary by cutoff, season, latitude, skin tone)
blocks.explanation: Estimates range from roughly a quarter to well over half of adults depending on the threshold and population — **~40%** is a defensible middle figure. The drivers are consistent: indoor life, sunscreen, higher latitudes, darker skin (more melanin = less synthesis), age (skin makes less with time), and the fact that almost no foods carry meaningful amounts.

blocks.title: What vitamin D actually does
blocks.simple: Vitamin D lets you absorb calcium from food and tells your immune system how to behave. Too little and your bones suffer and your immunity gets dysregulated.
blocks.mechanism: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to vitamin D3. The liver hydroxylates it to 25-hydroxy-vitamin D (25-OH-D, the storage form measured on blood tests), and the kidney converts that to 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D (calcitriol), the active hormone. Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor (VDR) — present in bone, gut, immune cells, muscle and more — acting as a transcription factor that regulates calcium absorption in the gut, bone remodeling, and immune-cell signaling.
blocks.studies: The bone role is rock-solid: severe deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, and D is required for dietary calcium absorption. Beyond bone, observational data link low 25-OH-D to many conditions, but large randomized trials (e.g. broad supplementation trials in already-replete populations) have mostly failed to show big reductions in cancer or cardiovascular events — the strongest case for supplementing is correcting a genuine deficiency, not megadosing a normal level.

blocks.title: D3 vs D2 — and its teammates

nodes.label: D3 (cholecalciferol)
