lessons.title: Red light & photobiomodulation
lessons.summary: Wavelengths, dose, and where the evidence is real versus marketing.

blocks.heading: Light as a tissue treatment
blocks.body: Red-light therapy — properly, **photobiomodulation (PBM)** — shines red (roughly **630–680 nm**) and near-infrared (roughly **800–880 nm**) light onto the body at low power. It isn't meant to heat you like a sauna, and it isn't about your eyes or body clock like a light box. The claim is that the light acts on the cells it reaches.

blocks.title: How it's supposed to work
blocks.simple: Certain wavelengths are absorbed by a part of your cells' energy machinery. The idea is that this nudges cells in the lit tissue to make energy and calm inflammation.
blocks.mechanism: The leading hypothesis centres on **cytochrome c oxidase**, a mitochondrial enzyme that absorbs red and near-infrared light. Absorption may release nitric oxide from it, raising energy (ATP) production and triggering short bursts of cell signaling. Red light is absorbed mostly in skin; near-infrared reaches somewhat deeper, but intensity falls off quickly with depth — one reason whole-body 'systemic' claims are hard to support.
blocks.studies: The mechanism rests mainly on cell and animal work. The dose response is **biphasic**: too little does nothing, and too much can cancel the effect (Huang, Chen, Carroll & Hamblin, Dose-Response, 2009). Clinical trials vary wildly in wavelength, power and schedule, which makes them hard to pool — and makes both 'red light works' and 'red light doesn't work' too simple.

blocks.title: Dose = power × time
blocks.body: What counts is the dose reaching your skin. **Irradiance** is power per area (mW/cm²); **fluence** is energy per area (J/cm²). Fluence = irradiance in mW/cm² × seconds ÷ 1,000. Irradiance drops sharply as you move away from a panel, so the distance you actually use matters as much as the LED count.

blocks.prompt: At your treatment distance a panel delivers 50 mW/cm². How much energy per area does a 10-minute session deliver?
blocks.explanation: 50 mW/cm² × 600 seconds = 30,000 mJ/cm² = 30 J/cm². Clinical protocols vary widely, often from a few to a few tens of J/cm² per session — and because the response is biphasic, doubling your time doesn't guarantee double the benefit.

blocks.title: Where the evidence stands

nodes.label: Stronger: mouth sores in cancer care
nodes.detail: International supportive-care guidelines (MASCC/ISOO) recommend intraoral photobiomodulation to help prevent oral mucositis in some cancer treatments, such as stem-cell transplant. Delivered by clinicians, not a home panel — but proof PBM can do something real.

nodes.label: Moderate: pattern hair loss
nodes.detail: Double-blind trials against sham devices show increased hair density with home laser/LED caps and combs, and meta-analyses agree. Several devices are FDA-cleared for it. Gains are modest and take months of consistent use.

nodes.label: Moderate: fine lines & skin texture
nodes.detail: Controlled trials — including one of 136 volunteers with twice-weekly sessions — reported less skin roughness, fewer fine lines and higher collagen density (Wunsch & Matuschka, Photomedicine and Laser Surgery, 2014). Effects are modest, and many studies are small or industry-linked.

nodes.label: Mixed: pain & sports recovery
nodes.detail: Some trials in neck pain, tendon problems and exercise recovery are positive and others aren't. Protocols are inconsistent and quality varies.

nodes.label: Weak: whole-body claims
nodes.detail: Testosterone, fat loss, thyroid, 'detox', immunity or longevity from a body panel: little or no good human evidence. Treat these as marketing.

blocks.body: ⚕️ Eye safety: near-infrared is invisible, so your blink reflex won't protect you, and high-power panels are intensely bright up close. Don't look into the LEDs, and wear goggles rated for the device's wavelengths, especially for face treatments. Check with a clinician first if you take light-sensitizing medication, have a light-sensitive condition or eye disease, are pregnant, or would be treating over a known or suspected cancer.

blocks.title: Reading a red-light spec sheet
items: Wavelengths in nm that match the studies for your goal — red around 630–680, near-infrared around 800–880.
Irradiance at a stated, realistic distance (such as 15 cm / 6 in), not only at the panel surface.
How irradiance was measured — inexpensive solar power meters can overstate LED output; spectroradiometer data is more trustworthy.
A 510(k) number and its actual indication, if clearance is claimed.
A timer and flicker-free output. Ignore LED count, 'watts' and 'clinical grade' as stand-ins for dose.

blocks.question: Which red-light claim has the strongest support?
options: Raising testosterone with a full-body panel
Increasing hair density in pattern hair loss with a cleared device
Detoxifying the body
Burning body fat
blocks.explanation: Pattern hair loss has multiple sham-controlled trials and FDA-cleared home devices behind it. The systemic claims — hormones, detox, fat loss — lack good human evidence.

lessons.title: Bright light therapy: the well-proven one
lessons.summary: 10,000 lux in the morning — how it works, who it helps, and how to use a light box.

blocks.heading: Not red light — a signal to your brain
blocks.body: A **light box** works through your **eyes**, not your skin. Bright light reaches specialised light-sensitive cells in the retina — most responsive to blue-ish light — that report straight to your brain's master clock, shifting circadian timing and influencing mood systems. A red panel can't do this job (those cells respond poorly to deep red), and a light box doesn't do what red-light therapy claims. Different tools, different evidence.

blocks.label: The best-studied dose for seasonal affective disorder: about 10,000 lux of white light at the eyes for roughly 30 minutes, soon after waking. For comparison, a bright indoor room is usually only a few hundred lux.

blocks.prompt: A dimmer box gives 2,500 lux at your eyes. Roughly how long would a session need to be to match the classic dose?
blocks.explanation: Dose is intensity × time: the classic protocols were ~10,000 lux for 30 minutes or ~2,500 lux for about 2 hours. That's why a small lamp that only reaches 10,000 lux a few centimetres from your face is a poor buy — you won't sit that close for long.

blocks.title: How strong is the evidence?
blocks.simple: For winter depression, bright light is one of the best-supported non-drug treatments there is, with effects comparable to antidepressant medication in controlled trials. It has also shown benefit in non-seasonal depression.
blocks.mechanism: Winter depression is often tied to a body clock that drifts later as mornings get darker. Morning light shifts the clock earlier and acts on mood-regulating pathways through the retina's direct connections to the brain. Timing matters: morning light moves your clock earlier; late-evening light pushes it later.
blocks.studies: A meta-analysis of randomized trials found bright light for seasonal depression — and for non-seasonal depression — had effect sizes similar to most antidepressant drug trials, while noting that only about 13% of the studies met its quality criteria (Golden et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2005). In a placebo-controlled trial in non-seasonal major depression, 10,000 lux for 30 minutes each morning beat placebo both alone and combined with fluoxetine, while fluoxetine alone did not beat placebo (Lam et al., JAMA Psychiatry, 2016).

blocks.title: Using a light box well
items: Use it daily within about an hour of waking — ~30 minutes at 10,000 lux, or as your clinician advises.
Sit at the distance where your box actually delivers 10,000 lux — check the manual.
Keep your eyes open with the light in view, slightly above and in front of you. Don't stare into it; read or eat breakfast.
If winter low mood returns every year, start as the days shorten and continue through the dark months.
Avoid late-evening sessions unless advised — they can push your sleep later.
Give it a couple of weeks. If you're not improving, or feel worse, see a clinician.

blocks.body: ⚕️ See a clinician before starting if you have **bipolar disorder** (light can trigger hypomania or mania), eye disease such as macular degeneration or diabetic retinopathy, a light-sensitive condition, or take light-sensitizing medication. Depression is a medical condition: use light alongside care, not instead of it, and seek help urgently if you have thoughts of self-harm. Headache, eye strain, nausea or feeling wired are common at first and usually settle.

blocks.title: What to look for in a light box
blocks.body: **10,000 lux at a stated, practical distance**; white light with **UV filtered out**; and a surface big enough that small head movements don't take you out of the beam. Colour-changing 'mood' lamps and ordinary daylight bulbs don't qualify — looking bright isn't the same as 10,000 lux at your eyes.

blocks.question: You want to treat winter low mood. Which option matches the evidence?
options: A 660 nm red-light panel on your chest
A 10,000-lux white light box used in the morning
A PEMF mat on an 'alpha wave' setting
A warm, dim lamp in the evening
blocks.explanation: Bright white light at the eyes in the morning is the studied treatment. Red light acts (if at all) on the skin it reaches, not your body clock, and evening light pushes your rhythm the wrong way.

blocks.label: Go deeper on light and your body clock
blocks.body: Free outdoor morning light, dim evenings and a fixed wake time — the Sleep track covers the daily light habits a box builds on.

lessons.title: PEMF: medical devices vs wellness mats
lessons.summary: A few regulated prescription uses, a lot of wellness marketing, and firm rules about implants.

blocks.heading: One acronym, very different devices
blocks.body: **Pulsed electromagnetic field** devices send pulsing current through coils to create a changing magnetic field, which induces tiny electrical currents in tissue. The label covers prescription bone-healing devices, cleared post-surgical devices, and consumer mats, belts and pads sold for 'wellness' — plus a much stronger clinic technology often mentioned in the same breath. Evidence for one says little about another.

blocks.title: From regulated to marketed

nodes.label: Bone growth stimulators (prescription)
nodes.detail: Prescribed for fractures that haven't healed (nonunions) and as an add-on after some spinal fusions. They are prescription medical devices, reviewed by the FDA for that specific use. Trial results are supportive but inconsistent.

nodes.label: Post-operative pain & swelling (cleared)
nodes.detail: Some prescription PEMF devices are FDA-cleared as an add-on for relieving post-operative pain and swelling in superficial soft tissue.

nodes.label: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (clinic)
nodes.detail: Not a wellness device: a far stronger, focused magnetic pulse that makes brain cells fire, FDA-cleared for depression and given by clinicians. Its evidence does **not** transfer to home mats, which are orders of magnitude weaker.

nodes.label: Wellness mats, belts & pads
nodes.detail: Low-intensity consumer devices sold for relaxation, sleep, recovery or 'cellular energy'. Small trials exist for uses like knee osteoarthritis pain, with mixed results and generally low quality. Claims tied to specific 'brainwave' or 'Earth resonance' frequencies aren't backed by good human evidence.

blocks.title: Evidence doesn't travel between devices
blocks.body: A bone stimulator's regulatory history tells you nothing about a mat: different field strengths, pulse shapes, body areas, conditions and patients. Always ask **which device, for which condition, tested against what sham?**

⚕️ Do not use a PEMF device if you have a **pacemaker, implanted defibrillator, cochlear implant, neurostimulator, insulin pump or any other implanted electronic device** — magnetic fields can interfere with them. Avoid it during pregnancy, and check with a clinician first if you have epilepsy, a bleeding disorder or cancer.

blocks.title: An honest evidence rating
blocks.simple: For a home PEMF mat, the honest rating is **low**: plausible biology, a few small positive trials, and marketing that goes far beyond them.
blocks.mechanism: Changing magnetic fields really do induce currents in tissue, and in cell and animal studies PEMF can influence signaling linked to bone formation and inflammation. But the parameters — frequency, intensity, waveform, duration — matter enormously, and consumer products rarely publish enough to compare with the studies.
blocks.studies: Bone-healing trials, the most established use, have been reviewed as promising but inconsistent. Knee osteoarthritis trials are small and mixed, and recent meta-analyses disagree on whether pain and function meaningfully improve. PEMF is easy to test against a sham device, so the scarcity of large, independent trials for wellness claims is itself informative.

blocks.title: If you still want to try one
items: Rule out implanted devices and pregnancy first.
Look for published field intensity (microtesla or gauss) and frequency — not just named 'presets'.
If clearance is claimed, look up the 510(k) and read the actual indication.
Treat it as a comfort or relaxation aid — not a replacement for care for pain, low mood, sleep problems or bone injuries.
Check the return policy, set a 4–6 week trial, and judge it by something concrete, like a pain score or a walk you can manage.

blocks.question: Which statement about PEMF is accurate?
options: Home PEMF mats are FDA-approved for depression
Prescription bone stimulators have a regulatory track record for non-healing fractures, but that doesn't validate wellness mats
PEMF is fine with a pacemaker because the fields are weak
Specific 'brainwave' frequencies are proven to improve sleep
blocks.explanation: The regulated PEMF uses are specific prescription devices for specific conditions. Clinic TMS for depression is a different, far stronger technology. Implanted electronics are a firm no, and frequency-specific wellness claims lack good evidence.

blocks.label: Browse PEMF devices with a sceptical eye
blocks.body: Check intensity, frequency and any clearance number — and skip the category entirely if you have an implanted device.

lessons.title: Build your therapy routine
lessons.summary: Rank by evidence per hour and dollar, fit it around sleep and training — or skip it.

blocks.heading: The garnish, not the meal
blocks.body: None of these devices comes close to the effect of regular exercise, enough sleep, not smoking and a decent diet. Even in the Finnish sauna cohort, the lowest risk of sudden cardiac death was in men who were **both** fit **and** frequent sauna users. Therapies are worth adding when the foundations are in place — and only if you'll actually use them.

blocks.title: Evidence per hour and dollar — a rough ranking

nodes.label: 1. Morning daylight — free
nodes.detail: Outdoor light soon after waking anchors your body clock and supports mood and sleep. No purchase needed.

nodes.label: 2. Light box — for winter low mood
nodes.detail: Inexpensive, 30 minutes you can pair with breakfast, and the best-proven device on this shelf for its specific use.

nodes.label: 3. Traditional sauna — if you can use one often
nodes.detail: The strongest long-term association data, but observational and time-hungry: 3–4 sessions a week is roughly an hour or more of heat, plus warm-up and cool-down time. A gym or public sauna tests the habit before you buy.

nodes.label: 4. Cold exposure — for alertness, soreness or enjoyment
nodes.detail: Cheap to try with cold showers. Short-term effects are real; long-term health effects are unproven, and badly timed cold can blunt strength gains.

nodes.label: 5. Red light — for a specific skin or hair goal
nodes.detail: Moderate evidence for targeted uses with the right device and dose; weak for whole-body claims.

nodes.label: 6. PEMF wellness mats — lowest
nodes.detail: Little good evidence for general wellness claims. The regulated uses are prescription devices.

blocks.title: Fitting therapies around sleep and training
items: Put bright light and cold earlier in the day — both are alerting.
A sauna or warm bath can help you fall asleep as your core temperature falls afterward; finish it an hour or two before bed.
If muscle growth is a goal, keep cold plunges off strength days or well separated from lifting — the ideal gap hasn't been established.
Sauna after training is fine: rehydrate, and keep alcohol out of it.
Never let a therapy session eat into the time you'd spend exercising or sleeping.

blocks.title: When to skip them entirely
blocks.body: Skip or pause therapies if you're not yet getting 7+ hours of sleep or exercising regularly (fix those first), if any contraindication in this track applies to you, if you're pregnant or trying to conceive (heat especially), or if the purchase would strain your budget. None of them is essential.

blocks.question: Sam sleeps 6 hours a night, doesn't exercise, and is deciding between an expensive home sauna and a cold plunge. What's the best next step?
options: Buy the sauna — it has the best evidence
Buy both and alternate them
Fix sleep and start exercising first, and test the habit cheaply with a gym sauna or cold showers
Buy a PEMF mat instead — it's the most convenient
blocks.explanation: Sleep and exercise dwarf any therapy's likely effect, and the sauna evidence itself is strongest alongside fitness. Trying a gym sauna or cold showers first shows whether the habit sticks before spending thousands.

blocks.body: Test before you buy: a few weeks of gym or public sauna visits, cold-finished showers, or morning walks will tell you whether you'll keep the habit — the best predictor of whether a device earns its price.

blocks.label: Browse the Therapies shelf
blocks.body: Compare saunas, cold plunges, light boxes, red-light panels and PEMF devices using the specs and red flags from this track.

blocks.label: Lay the foundations first
blocks.body: Training is the lever every therapy on this shelf is trying to imitate — start there.

personal-care.title: Personal Care
personal-care.intro: Your skin, hair and teeth are organs you maintain every day — and the personal-care aisle is where marketing outruns evidence fastest. This track separates the few habits with strong evidence (daily sunscreen, a retinoid, fluoride, cleaning between your teeth) from the claims that don't hold up, and teaches you to read a label, weigh a safety scare, and know when to see a clinician.

lessons.title: Why personal care is a longevity habit
lessons.summary: Skin is an organ, UV is its main ager, and your gums are linked to the rest of you — with caveats.

blocks.heading: More than cosmetics
blocks.body:
Your skin is your largest organ — a barrier that holds water in, keeps microbes and irritants out, helps control temperature, and makes vitamin D. Your mouth is the entry point to your gut, and for many adults a site of low-grade, long-running inflammation.

Most of the personal-care aisle is about how you look and feel, and that's fine. But a few habits in it have **strong evidence for health outcomes**: preventing skin cancer, keeping your teeth, and controlling gum inflammation. This track is about telling those apart from the marketing.

blocks.title: Two kinds of skin aging
blocks.body: **Intrinsic aging** — genes and time — is slow, and mostly shows as thinner skin with fine lines. **Extrinsic aging**, driven mainly by UV light (photoaging) and smoking, causes the deep wrinkles, leathery texture, uneven pigment and broken capillaries most people picture when they think of 'old skin'. The second kind is largely preventable.

blocks.label: A delivery-truck driver's face after 28 years at the wheel: the left side, next to the side window, was visibly thicker, more wrinkled and more sun-damaged than the right. It's a single case, but a vivid one — glass blocks UVB, while car side windows in one study of 29 cars blocked only about 71% of UVA on average, versus about 96% for windshields.
blocks.source: Gordon & Brieva, NEJM 2012; Boxer Wachler, JAMA Ophthalmology 2016

blocks.prompt: A study of 298 women in sunny southern France estimated what share of visible facial aging signs was attributable to sun exposure?
blocks.explanation: The estimate was about 80% (Flament et al., Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology 2013). Treat the exact number as a ballpark: it's one observational study of light-skinned women, run by researchers at a cosmetics company. The direction, though, is backed by much stronger evidence — including the randomized trial in the next lesson, where daily sunscreen measurably slowed skin aging.

blocks.title: How UV ages skin
blocks.simple: UVB burns the surface. UVA reaches deeper, is present all year and passes through glass. Both damage DNA and slowly break down the collagen and elastic fibers that keep skin firm and smooth.
blocks.mechanism: UV generates reactive oxygen species and directly damages DNA. In the dermis it switches on enzymes called matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade collagen, while reducing new collagen production. Repeated over decades, the damage is imperfectly repaired, and tangled, abnormal elastic material accumulates (solar elastosis). The same DNA damage in surface cells drives skin cancer, which is why the anti-aging and anti-cancer benefits of sun protection travel together.
blocks.studies: Fisher and colleagues (Nature, 1996) showed that UVB induces collagen-degrading MMPs in human skin within hours, at doses well below those that turn skin red — so damage accumulates without a sunburn. The same study found pre-treating skin with retinoic acid (tretinoin) largely blocked that induction. The strongest outcome evidence for prevention comes from the Nambour randomized trial of daily sunscreen, covered in lesson 2.

blocks.heading: Your gums and your body: association vs causation
blocks.body:
Periodontitis — chronic infection and inflammation that destroys the gum and bone anchoring your teeth — affects more than 40% of US adults over 30. People who have it also have higher rates of heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes.

But **associated is not the same as caused.** Smoking, diabetes, age and income raise the risk of both gum disease and heart disease. A scientific statement from the American Heart Association (Lockhart et al., Circulation 2012) concluded that a cause-and-effect link to cardiovascular disease **has not been established**, and that there is no evidence treating gum disease prevents it. The diabetes link is firmer: in randomized trials, treating periodontitis modestly lowered blood sugar (lesson 8).

blocks.question: People with gum disease have more heart attacks. What does the evidence currently support?
options: Gum disease is proven to cause heart attacks
Treating gum disease is proven to prevent heart attacks
They're consistently associated, but shared risk factors like smoking and diabetes may explain part of it — causation isn't established
There's no connection at all
blocks.explanation: The association is real and consistent, and there are plausible mechanisms (bacteria and inflammation entering the bloodstream). But no trial has shown that treating gums prevents heart attacks or strokes. Look after your gums for your teeth and your blood sugar; treat the heart benefit as promising but unproven.

lessons.title: Sunscreen: the evidence and how to use it
lessons.summary: The one skincare product with randomized-trial evidence for cancer and aging — if you apply enough.

blocks.heading: A skincare product with a real trial
blocks.body:
In 1992, 1,621 adults in Nambour, Queensland, were randomized either to apply an SPF 15+ broad-spectrum sunscreen to their head, neck, arms and hands every morning, or to keep using sunscreen however they liked. The trial ran for 4.5 years, and researchers kept following participants long afterward.

- **Squamous-cell carcinoma** was about 39% less common in the daily group. Basal-cell carcinoma was not significantly reduced (Green et al., Lancet 1999).
- **Melanoma:** ten years after the trial ended, the daily group had half as many new melanomas (11 vs 22, a borderline result statistically) and far fewer invasive ones (3 vs 11) (Green et al., Journal of Clinical Oncology 2011).
- **Skin aging:** daily users showed no detectable increase in skin aging over 4.5 years, and were 24% less likely to show increased aging than the comparison group (Hughes et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2013).

blocks.title: Daily beats occasional
blocks.body: Nambour didn't compare sunscreen with no sunscreen — it compared a **daily morning habit** with 'whenever you think of it'. The habit was the intervention. Put it next to brushing your teeth, not in your beach bag.

blocks.title: Reading a sunscreen label

nodes.label: SPF
nodes.detail: Measures protection against UVB (the burning rays), tested at 2 mg of product per cm² of skin. SPF 15 blocks about 93% of UVB, SPF 30 about 97%, SPF 50 about 98%. Higher numbers add little on paper, but they give you a margin when you under-apply — which almost everyone does.

nodes.label: Broad spectrum
nodes.detail: In the US, 'broad spectrum' means the product passed a UVA test (a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm). Without it, a high SPF can still let a lot of UVA through.

nodes.label: UVA logo / PA rating
nodes.detail: In the EU, 'UVA' in a circle means UVA protection is at least one-third of the SPF. Many Asian labels use PA+ to PA++++ — more plus signs, more UVA protection.

nodes.label: Water resistant (40 or 80 min)
nodes.detail: US labels may claim 40 or 80 minutes of water resistance. 'Waterproof', 'sweatproof' and 'sunblock' aren't permitted claims. Reapply after that time, or after towelling off.

nodes.label: Expiry
nodes.detail: US sunscreens must stay at full strength for at least 3 years or carry an expiry date. Heat degrades them, so don't store a bottle in a hot car.

blocks.prompt: About how many teaspoons of sunscreen does it take to cover an adult's whole body at the thickness SPF is tested at?
blocks.explanation: Roughly 30 mL — about 6 teaspoons — for an adult body in swimwear. Studies find people typically apply somewhere between a quarter and a half of the tested amount, and at a quarter of the dose the real protection can fall to about a quarter of the SPF on the label. For the face and neck, plan on roughly a quarter to half a teaspoon.

blocks.title: How to actually use it
items: Use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher whenever the UV index is 3 or above — in many places, that's most days of the year.
Apply generously to all exposed skin, including ears, the back of the neck, the backs of your hands and any scalp part.
Reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors, and after swimming, heavy sweating or towelling.
Treat sunscreen as one layer: shade around midday, a wide-brimmed hat, UV-blocking sunglasses and clothing do a lot of the work.
SPF in makeup or tinted moisturizer only counts if you apply a full dose — which you almost never do with makeup.
Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun rather than relying on sunscreen, and ask a pediatrician before using it on them.

blocks.title: Mineral vs chemical filters — and the absorption debate
blocks.simple: Mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and organic or 'chemical' filters both work. The best sunscreen is the one you'll wear every day in the right amount. Mineral filters are the natural pick for sensitive skin, or if you want the filters with the most regulatory certainty.
blocks.mechanism: Despite the common claim that minerals 'reflect' UV, both types protect mainly by absorbing it — lab measurements put reflection from zinc oxide and titanium dioxide at only about 4–5%. Zinc oxide covers UVB and UVA well; titanium dioxide is weaker in UVA. Organic filters are combined for coverage: avobenzone, for example, is a strong UVA filter that needs stabilizing. Mineral formulas can leave a white cast; tinted versions with iron oxides also block some visible light, which matters for people with melasma.
blocks.studies: In FDA-run randomized studies (Matta et al., JAMA 2019 and 2020), volunteers applied sunscreen at the full tested amount to most of their body, and six common organic filters — avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate — reached blood levels above the threshold at which FDA asks for further safety testing. That threshold is a trigger for more study, not a finding of harm, and the authors said people should keep using sunscreen. In 2019 FDA proposed that only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide had enough data to be 'generally recognized as safe and effective', and asked for more data on most organic filters rather than declaring them unsafe. In June 2026 FDA added bemotrizinol, a broad-spectrum filter long used in Europe and Asia, to the US sunscreen monograph (at up to 6%) — the first new US sunscreen ingredient in more than two decades. Hawaii has banned sales of sunscreens with oxybenzone and octinoxate since 2021 over coral-reef concerns; that reef evidence comes largely from lab studies, and 'reef safe' is an unregulated label.

blocks.body: Some medicines make you burn much faster — including doxycycline and other tetracyclines, some diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, oral isotretinoin, and topical retinoids. If you take one, ask your pharmacist and be stricter with protection. And no sunscreen makes tanning beds safe: the WHO's cancer agency (IARC) classifies UV tanning devices as carcinogenic to humans.

blocks.label: Compare sunscreens
blocks.body: Browse the body-care shelf for broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreens. Check the filters, the water-resistance claim, and — most important — whether it's a texture you'll wear every day. Worried about vitamin D? A 2019 review in the British Journal of Dermatology found little evidence that real-world sunscreen use lowers vitamin D levels; if you're concerned, test your level rather than skip protection.

lessons.title: The actives with real evidence
lessons.summary: Retinoids, vitamin C, niacinamide, acids and azelaic acid — what each does, at what strength, and how long to wait.

blocks.heading: A short list with trials behind it
blocks.body:
Thousands of ingredients are marketed as 'actives'. Only a handful have controlled human trials showing visible effects on sun damage, pigment or acne. Sunscreen **prevents** damage; these **repair or treat** — modestly and slowly.

Expect weeks before you notice anything and months for the full effect. Be wary of any serum that promises visible results by the weekend.

blocks.title: The evidence-backed actives

nodes.label: Retinoids
nodes.detail: The best-studied topical for sun-damaged skin. **Tretinoin** (prescription) has vehicle-controlled trials showing smoother, less wrinkled, more even skin. **Retinol** (non-prescription, commonly 0.1–1%) has to be converted in the skin to the active form, so it's gentler and weaker. **Adapalene 0.1%** is sold without a prescription in the US for acne. Expect dryness and peeling for the first 2–4 weeks, and visible change over 3–6 months.

nodes.label: Vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid)
nodes.detail: An antioxidant that supports collagen formation and modestly fades pigment. Pure L-ascorbic acid gets into skin best in acidic formulas at concentrations up to about 20%. It oxidizes — a serum that has turned dark orange-brown has lost potency. Derivatives are more stable, but in lab absorption tests several common ones didn't raise skin vitamin C levels the same way.

nodes.label: Niacinamide
nodes.detail: Vitamin B3. At 2–5% it's well tolerated, and trials show modest improvements in blotchy pigment, redness, sallowness and fine lines over about 8–12 weeks — much of that research funded by manufacturers. Higher is not clearly better: very high-percentage serums mainly add irritation risk.

nodes.label: AHAs & BHA
nodes.detail: **Glycolic and lactic acid** (AHAs) loosen dead surface cells for smoother texture and brighter tone; US safety reviewers consider consumer AHA products safe up to 10% at a pH of 3.5 or higher. **Salicylic acid** (BHA, 0.5–2%) is oil-soluble, gets into pores, and is an approved non-prescription acne active. AHAs make skin more sun-sensitive while you use them and for about a week after.

nodes.label: Azelaic acid
nodes.detail: Calms the redness and bumps of rosacea, treats acne, and fades post-acne marks and melasma. The 15% and 20% versions are prescription in the US; lower-strength cosmetic versions exist. It's often considered compatible with pregnancy — confirm with your clinician.

nodes.label: Benzoyl peroxide
nodes.detail: A non-prescription acne active (2.5–10%) that kills acne bacteria. Lower strengths irritate less and often work about as well. It bleaches towels and pillowcases.

blocks.label: was all it took, in a double-blind trial against a plain cream, for topical tretinoin to visibly improve sun-damaged facial skin. The trial was small, but larger trials since have confirmed it, and tretinoin remains the reference treatment for photoaged skin.

blocks.title: Retinol vs tretinoin
blocks.simple: Tretinoin is retinoic acid itself — the form skin cells actually respond to. Retinol is a precursor your skin has to convert, so it's gentler and slower, but it still has controlled-trial evidence.
blocks.mechanism: Retinoic acid binds nuclear receptors (RARs) that switch on genes for cell turnover and collagen production, and it blocks UV-triggered collagen-degrading enzymes. Retinol is converted in two steps (retinol to retinaldehyde to retinoic acid), and only part of it makes it through — which is why it irritates less and acts more slowly. Retinaldehyde products sit in between.
blocks.studies: Tretinoin's evidence for photoaging dates to vehicle-controlled trials in the late 1980s (Weiss et al., JAMA 1988) and has been confirmed repeatedly. For retinol, a randomized, vehicle-controlled trial in elderly adults (mean age 87) found 0.4% retinol applied up to three times a week reduced fine wrinkling on the arm over 24 weeks (Kafi et al., Archives of Dermatology 2007). Head-to-head evidence comparing typical over-the-counter retinol serums with tretinoin is thin, and most retinol product claims rest on manufacturer-run studies.

blocks.prompt: Pure vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid) only gets into skin from an acidic formula. Below roughly what pH?
blocks.explanation: Lab absorption studies found L-ascorbic acid has to be formulated below about pH 3.5 to enter skin, with uptake peaking around 20% concentration (Pinnell et al., Dermatologic Surgery 2001). That acidity is also why vitamin C serums can sting, and why many gentler 'vitamin C' products use derivatives instead — which have less evidence behind them.

blocks.body: **Pregnant, trying to conceive, or breastfeeding?** Avoid topical retinoids — retinol, retinaldehyde, adapalene, tretinoin, tazarotene — unless a clinician approves. Oral retinoids cause birth defects, and topical ones are avoided as a precaution. Tretinoin, tazarotene, prescription-strength azelaic acid and stronger acne treatments are prescription products for a reason: get them through a clinician, who can also check whether your 'acne' or 'wrinkles' is actually rosacea, dermatitis or something else.

blocks.question: Ten days after starting a retinoid, your skin is dry and flaky. What's the most reasonable response?
options: It isn't working — stop and switch products
It's normal early irritation — drop to every second or third night, use a pea-sized amount, add moisturizer, and it usually settles within a few weeks
Apply it twice a day to push through faster
It means you're allergic and can never use retinoids
blocks.explanation: Dryness, peeling and mild stinging in the first 2–4 weeks are expected as skin adjusts. Cut the frequency, use a pea-sized amount for the whole face, and buffer with moisturizer. Stop and see a clinician if you get swelling, blistering, or a rash spreading beyond where you applied it.

blocks.label: Browse skincare by active
blocks.body: Favor products that disclose the active's concentration. A retinoid, vitamin C or niacinamide percentage on the label tells you more than a long list of trendy extracts.

lessons.title: A minimal routine that protects your barrier
lessons.summary: Cleanse, moisturize, protect — then add one active at a time.

blocks.heading: Three steps do most of the work
blocks.body:
A good routine is short.

- **Morning:** a gentle cleanse (or just water), moisturizer if you need it, sunscreen.
- **Evening:** cleanse off sunscreen and the day, apply your one active if you use one, moisturize.

Everything beyond that is optional — and every extra product is another chance for irritation or allergy.

blocks.title: Your barrier is bricks and mortar
blocks.body: The outermost layer of skin is flattened dead cells (the bricks) held together by a mortar of ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids. It keeps water in and irritants out. Harsh cleansers, over-exfoliation and piling on actives strip that mortar — and the result is tightness, stinging, redness and breakouts that people often try to fix with *more* products.

blocks.prompt: Healthy skin's surface is slightly acidic. What is its natural pH, on average?
blocks.explanation: A study of 330 people estimated natural skin surface pH averages about 4.7 (Lambers et al., International Journal of Cosmetic Science 2006). Traditional bar soaps are alkaline, often around pH 9–10, which is one reason they can leave skin tight and dry. Synthetic-detergent ('syndet') bars and gentle liquid cleansers sit much closer to skin's own pH.

blocks.title: Build it one step at a time
items: Cleanser: gentle and fragrance-free; lukewarm water; pat dry rather than rub.
Moisturizer: choose by texture — gel or lotion for oily skin, cream for dry. Look for humectants (glycerin, hyaluronic acid) plus barrier lipids (ceramides) or occlusives (petrolatum, dimethicone).
Sunscreen every morning, as the last step.
Add one new product at a time, and wait 2–4 weeks before adding another, so you know what caused any reaction.
Start retinoids and acids 2–3 nights a week, then build up as your skin tolerates them.
Moisturize within a few minutes of washing, while skin is still slightly damp.

blocks.title: Layering: what goes with what

nodes.label: Order
nodes.detail: Thinnest to thickest: watery serums first, creams after, sunscreen last in the morning. For prescription treatments, follow your prescriber's instructions.

nodes.label: Retinoid + AHA/BHA
nodes.detail: Using both on the same night means more irritation, especially at the start. Alternate nights instead.

nodes.label: Benzoyl peroxide + tretinoin
nodes.detail: Benzoyl peroxide can break down traditional tretinoin, so use them at different times of day unless a product is formulated to combine them. Adapalene is stable alongside benzoyl peroxide.

nodes.label: Vitamin C + niacinamide
nodes.detail: The old warning against combining them comes from lab conditions (heat, older formulations), and many dermatologists now consider them compatible. If the pair makes you flush or sting, use them at different times of day.

nodes.label: Vitamin C + sunscreen
nodes.detail: A sensible morning pair: antioxidants may add some defense against UV-generated free radicals. They never replace sunscreen.

blocks.body: **Patch test before it goes on your face.** The American Academy of Dermatology's method: apply the product to a quarter-sized spot on the inside of your arm or the bend of your elbow, twice a day for 7–10 days, leaving it on as long as you normally would. No redness, itching or swelling? Go ahead. It isn't a guarantee — facial skin is more sensitive, and allergies can develop after months of use — but it catches many problems early.

blocks.question: You added an acid toner, a retinol and a new vitamin C serum in the same week. Now everything stings and your skin looks red and tight. Best next step?
options: Add a stronger exfoliant to clear the dead skin
Stop the actives, go back to gentle cleanser, plain moisturizer and sunscreen until it calms, then reintroduce one product at a time
Replace every product with a different brand
Keep going — stinging means it's working
blocks.explanation: This is a classic compromised barrier. Stripping back lets it repair, usually over days to a couple of weeks. Reintroducing products one at a time, weeks apart, tells you which one was the problem — something you can't learn by swapping everything at once.

blocks.body: See a dermatologist if irritation doesn't settle within a couple of weeks of stripping back; if you get swelling of the eyelids or lips, blistering or oozing; or if your 'breakouts' are really persistent redness, flushing or scaly patches. Those can be allergic contact dermatitis, rosacea, eczema or psoriasis — conditions that need a diagnosis, not more products.

lessons.title: Reading a label
lessons.summary: Ingredient order, the Drug Facts box, allergens, and the marketing words with no legal meaning.

blocks.heading: The back of the pack is the real product
blocks.body:
The front of a pack is advertising. The back — the ingredient list, and on some products a Drug Facts panel — is regulated. Three rules get you most of the way:

- **Ingredients are listed in descending order of concentration**, using standardized INCI names (Aqua is water, Parfum is fragrance, Tocopherol is vitamin E).
- **At 1% or less, order is free.** An extract listed after the preservatives is likely present in tiny amounts, whatever the front of the pack implies.
- **In the US, sunscreens, antiperspirants, acne treatments and anti-dandruff products are OTC drugs.** Their active ingredients and percentages must appear in a Drug Facts box — the one place a concentration is legally required.

blocks.prompt: At or below what concentration may ingredients be listed in any order on US and EU cosmetic labels?
blocks.explanation: Above 1%, the order follows concentration; at 1% or below, manufacturers can list ingredients in any order. A handy landmark: preservatives such as phenoxyethanol are typically used at 1% or less, so anything listed after them is probably present in very small amounts.

blocks.title: Words that sound regulated but aren't

nodes.label: Clean / non-toxic
nodes.detail: No legal definition in the US or EU. Each retailer or brand writes its own list of excluded ingredients, usually based on hazard rather than dose.

nodes.label: Natural / chemical-free
nodes.detail: No legal definition for cosmetics in the US. Everything, including water, is a chemical — and 'natural' ingredients like essential oils are common allergens.

nodes.label: Hypoallergenic
nodes.detail: FDA tried to define it in the 1970s, and a federal appeals court struck the rule down in 1977. FDA says there are no federal standards: it means whatever the company wants it to mean.

nodes.label: Dermatologist tested
nodes.detail: No standard for how many dermatologists, what test, or what result was required. It can mean a small, company-run panel.

nodes.label: Clinically proven
nodes.detail: Often a small company-sponsored study with self-reported results, such as a percentage of users who 'felt' smoother skin. Look for how many people, for how long, whether there was a comparison group, and whether outcomes were measured rather than self-rated.

nodes.label: Non-comedogenic
nodes.detail: No required test behind the claim in the US. A hint at best — your own skin is the real test.

nodes.label: Organic
nodes.detail: The USDA organic seal on a cosmetic means its agricultural ingredients were certified to USDA standards; the word alone is harder to verify. Either way, organic says nothing about safety or effectiveness.

blocks.title: Fragrance is a black box
blocks.body: 'Fragrance' or 'Parfum' can stand for dozens of undisclosed components, and US labels can list it as a single word. The EU requires specific fragrance allergens to be named on the label above small thresholds — about two dozen for years, expanding to more than 80 under a 2023 rule that phases in from July 2026. If you react to many products, fragrance is one of the first things to rule out.

blocks.heading: Contact allergens worth recognizing
blocks.body:
- **Fragrance**, including 'natural' essential oils (lavender, tea tree, citrus), and named allergens such as linalool, limonene, geraniol, citronellol, eugenol and cinnamal — some become more allergenic once oxidized by air.
- **Preservatives:** methylisothiazolinone (banned from leave-on cosmetics in the EU since 2017 after a surge in allergy cases) and formaldehyde releasers such as DMDM hydantoin, quaternium-15, imidazolidinyl urea and diazolidinyl urea.
- **Hair dye:** p-phenylenediamine (PPD) — also found in illegal 'black henna' temporary tattoos, which can cause severe reactions and lifelong sensitization.
- **Others:** cocamidopropyl betaine (a foaming agent, largely via impurities), lanolin, propolis, and some sunscreen filters such as oxybenzone and octocrylene.

Once you're allergic to something, it's usually for life. Avoidance is the treatment, which is why reading the list matters.

blocks.question: A moisturizer says 'hypoallergenic' and 'dermatologist tested'. What does that guarantee?
options: It passed a standardized FDA allergy test
It contains no fragrance or common allergens
Nothing specific — neither term has a legal standard in the US
A dermatology panel approved it as safe for eczema
blocks.explanation: Neither claim has a federal definition or required test. A 'hypoallergenic' product can still contain fragrance or a known allergen. The ingredient list is the only reliable way to check.

blocks.body: Buying for sensitive skin? Look for **fragrance-free**, not 'unscented' — 'unscented' can mean a masking fragrance was added to cover the base smell. Then scan the list for the allergens above. A short ingredient list is also much easier to troubleshoot than a long one.

blocks.label: Practice on a real label
blocks.body: Open any product on the personal-care shelf and read its ingredient list: find the first five ingredients, the fragrance, the preservatives, and whether the active is disclosed at a percentage.

lessons.title: Ingredient safety without the fear
lessons.summary: Hazard isn't risk, how cosmetics are regulated, and what the evidence says about the usual suspects.

blocks.heading: The dose makes the risk
blocks.body:
Ingredient-scare lists and 'toxicity' ratings usually tell you whether a substance *can* cause harm at some dose, in some form, by some route. That's its **hazard**. What matters to you is **risk**: the hazard, times how much actually reaches you, times how often.

The WHO's cancer agency, IARC, classifies hazard, not risk. That's why processed meat and alcoholic drinks sit in the same top category as plutonium: the category says how confident the evidence is that something *can* cause cancer, not how dangerous everyday exposure is.

blocks.title: Three questions for any scary claim
blocks.body: **1. How much?** Was the dose anywhere near what's in the product and what gets through your skin? **2. In whom?** People, animals, or cells in a dish? **3. What outcome?** Actual disease — or just a substance detected in blood or a change in a lab marker?

blocks.title: How cosmetics are regulated
blocks.simple: In both the US and EU, cosmetics don't need approval before they go on sale — companies are responsible for making them safe. The EU has long had the more detailed system; the US tightened its rules significantly in 2022.
blocks.mechanism: **US:** cosmetics were governed for decades by a 1938 law that didn't require companies to register products or report injuries. The Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act (MoCRA), signed in December 2022, added facility registration and product listing, mandatory reporting of serious adverse events to FDA, a requirement to have evidence of safety, and FDA power to order recalls. It also directed FDA to write rules on manufacturing practices, fragrance-allergen labeling and asbestos testing for talc — rules that have been slow to arrive. Products that make drug claims (sunscreens, antiperspirants, acne and dandruff treatments) are regulated as OTC drugs. **EU:** every product needs a documented safety assessment and a named responsible person, and a long annex of prohibited substances — though many entries are substances nobody would put in a cosmetic, so viral 'the EU bans over a thousand ingredients, the US about a dozen' comparisons overstate the real gap.
blocks.studies: Regulators act ingredient by ingredient. The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety publishes opinions that drive concentration limits — for example, restricting certain parabens and banning methylisothiazolinone from leave-on products. In the US, FDA's proposed ban on formaldehyde in hair-straightening products has repeatedly missed its target dates, which is a good reminder that 'still on shelves' doesn't mean 'cleared as safe'.

blocks.title: The usual suspects: what the evidence says

nodes.label: Parabens
nodes.detail: Effective, inexpensive preservatives with weak estrogen-like activity in lab tests — thousands of times weaker than the body's own estrogen. A widely publicized 2004 study detected parabens in breast tumor tissue but measured no normal tissue for comparison and couldn't show they caused cancer. The EU banned five less-studied parabens and capped propyl- and butylparaben; methyl- and ethylparaben remain permitted. Paraben allergy is rare, and 'paraben-free' products need another preservative — sometimes a more common allergen.

nodes.label: Aluminum in antiperspirants
nodes.detail: The US National Cancer Institute says no scientific evidence links antiperspirants to breast cancer, and the suspected Alzheimer's link hasn't held up. The real caution is on the label: US antiperspirants tell people with kidney disease to ask a doctor first, because weakened kidneys clear aluminum poorly.

nodes.label: Sulfates (SLS, SLES)
nodes.detail: Effective detergents that can irritate dry, sensitive or eczema-prone skin, especially with long contact. Not a cancer or hormone concern. Choosing a milder cleanser is a comfort decision, not a safety one.

nodes.label: Oxybenzone
nodes.detail: Measurably absorbed and flagged by FDA for more data; the hormone concerns come mainly from animal studies at high doses. It's also one of the more common sunscreen allergens. Reasonable to prefer other filters — not a reason to skip sunscreen.

nodes.label: Talc
nodes.detail: The documented hazard is contamination with asbestos, which is why testing matters. In 2024 IARC classed talc as 'probably carcinogenic', based on limited human evidence — mainly a link between genital-area powder use and ovarian cancer that could reflect asbestos contamination or study bias — plus animal and mechanistic data. Avoiding loose talc powder in the genital area is a reasonable precaution.

nodes.label: Formaldehyde & releasers
nodes.detail: Formaldehyde is a known human carcinogen when inhaled at high exposures — a real concern with some keratin or 'smoothing' hair treatments that release fumes under a flat iron. The small amounts released by preservatives in everyday products are mainly an allergy issue.

blocks.body: The best-documented harms come from **unregulated or illegal products**, not mainstream preservatives: skin-lightening creams bought online that contain mercury or undisclosed steroids; over-the-counter hydroquinone, which hasn't been legally sold without a prescription in the US since 2020; 'black henna' containing PPD; and hair-smoothing treatments that release formaldehyde. If you've used any of these and have symptoms — or you're pregnant — stop and talk to a clinician.

blocks.prompt: Under MoCRA, how many business days does a US cosmetics company have to report a serious adverse event to FDA?
blocks.explanation: Before the 2022 law, reporting injuries from cosmetics was voluntary. Companies must now report serious adverse events — outcomes such as hospitalization or significant disfigurement, including serious burns, severe persistent rashes or significant hair loss — within 15 business days of learning about them. You can report a problem yourself, too, through FDA's MedWatch system.

blocks.question: A viral post says an ingredient in your shampoo is 'linked to cancer' because it caused tumors in rats fed high doses. What's the most useful follow-up question?
options: Is it a synthetic chemical?
How do the dose and route in that study compare with what actually reaches you from a rinse-off shampoo?
Is it banned somewhere in the world?
How many people shared the post?
blocks.explanation: Hazard shown by a high oral dose in animals says little about risk from a product that's diluted, on your scalp for a minute and rinsed away. Dose and route are what turn a hazard into a risk — or not. 'Synthetic' and 'banned somewhere' are poor shortcuts: many natural substances are hazardous, and bans often reflect precaution or trade rules rather than proven harm.

blocks.label: See how products are scored
blocks.body: The personal-care methodology page explains which ingredient flags — fragrance allergens, irritants, pore-cloggers and ingredients of concern — affect a product's score, and by how much.

lessons.title: Hair: what actually works
lessons.summary: Name the type of hair loss first — then minoxidil, the prescription options, and the long list that mostly doesn't work.

blocks.heading: Diagnosis before products
blocks.body:
'Hair loss' covers several conditions, and the right response depends on which one you have:

- **Pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia):** gradual thinning at the temples and crown in men, or a widening part in women. By far the most common; genetic and hormone-driven, and it progresses without treatment.
- **Telogen effluvium:** diffuse shedding that starts a few months after a shock — high fever, surgery, childbirth, crash dieting, severe stress, some medicines. Usually recovers once the trigger passes.
- **Alopecia areata:** smooth, round bald patches caused by the immune system attacking follicles.
- **Traction alopecia:** thinning along the hairline from tight braids, ponytails or extensions — reversible early, permanent if it goes on for years.
- **Scarring alopecias:** inflammation that permanently destroys follicles, sometimes with itching, burning, redness or scale. These need a dermatologist quickly.

blocks.prompt: After a high fever, surgery or childbirth, noticeable shedding (telogen effluvium) usually starts about how many months later?
blocks.explanation: A shock pushes many follicles into their resting phase at once, and those hairs fall out roughly 2–3 months later — which is why people rarely connect the shedding to its cause. It usually settles within about 6 months once the trigger is gone. Shedding that lasts longer deserves a check for thyroid problems, iron deficiency or medication effects.

blocks.label: more hair regrowth with 5% topical minoxidil than with 2% after 48 weeks, in a randomized trial of 393 men — with more scalp itching and irritation at the higher strength.
blocks.source: Olsen et al., Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology 2002

blocks.title: The options with real evidence
blocks.simple: Topical minoxidil, available without a prescription, is the first-line product for pattern hair loss in both men and women. Finasteride, a prescription pill, works for men. Everything works only for as long as you keep using it.
blocks.mechanism: Minoxidil lengthens the growth phase of hair follicles and enlarges shrunken ones, though exactly how is still not fully understood. Expect a temporary increase in shedding in the first weeks, first results after about 4 months, and a fair verdict at 6–12 months. Stop, and the gains fade over the following months. Finasteride blocks the enzyme (5-alpha reductase type II) that converts testosterone into DHT, the hormone that shrinks scalp follicles in pattern hair loss. Low-dose oral minoxidil is a prescription, off-label option dermatologists increasingly use.
blocks.studies: Topical 5% minoxidil beat both 2% and placebo in men (Olsen et al., 2002). Finasteride 1 mg daily slowed hair loss and increased hair counts versus placebo in two one-year trials of 1,553 men, with benefits maintained in a second year (Kaufman et al., Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology 1998). Low-level laser devices are FDA-cleared, and several mostly industry-funded trials show modest density gains. Microneedling combined with minoxidil has small trials suggesting extra benefit. The popular rosemary-oil claim rests largely on one small trial comparing it with low-strength 2% minoxidil.

blocks.body: **Finasteride and oral minoxidil are prescription drugs — use them only under a clinician's care, including when they come from a telehealth hair-loss service.** Finasteride can cause sexual side effects, and US and EU regulators list suicidal thoughts among its possible side effects. It lowers PSA readings, which matters for prostate screening, and it can harm a male fetus: anyone who is or may become pregnant shouldn't take it or handle crushed or broken tablets. In 2025 FDA warned about side effects reported with compounded topical finasteride, which has no FDA-approved version. Oral minoxidil can cause fluid retention, a fast heartbeat and unwanted body hair. Don't use minoxidil while pregnant or breastfeeding. And see a dermatologist for sudden or patchy loss, or a scalp that's painful, red or scaly.

blocks.title: What mostly doesn't work

nodes.label: Biotin supplements
nodes.detail: Biotin helps hair only if you're genuinely deficient, which is rare. High doses can also distort blood tests — including thyroid and troponin (heart attack) tests — which FDA has warned about. Tell your clinician before any blood work.

nodes.label: 'Growth' shampoos
nodes.detail: A shampoo sits on your scalp for a minute or two. Most growth claims rest on ingredients without controlled evidence. 'Thickening' shampoos can make hair look fuller by coating the strands — cosmetic, not regrowth. Ketoconazole shampoo has small studies hinting at a benefit in pattern hair loss, but its proven use is dandruff.

nodes.label: Hair gummies & collagen
nodes.detail: Unless you're low in something — iron, vitamin D, zinc, protein — there's little evidence extra nutrients grow hair. Too much vitamin A or selenium can actually cause hair loss.

nodes.label: Scalp 'detoxes'
nodes.detail: No good evidence that product residue or 'toxins' clog follicles and cause pattern hair loss.

blocks.heading: Scalp care that helps
blocks.body:
Dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis are driven partly by an overreaction to *Malassezia*, a yeast that lives on everyone's scalp. Anti-dandruff shampoos with **zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, ketoconazole, salicylic acid or coal tar** have evidence — leave the lather on for a few minutes, and alternate two actives if one stops working. Wash as often as your scalp needs; daily is fine for an oily scalp.

Heat styling and bleaching damage the hair shaft, and tight styles strain the follicle. Conditioner reduces breakage by cutting friction.

blocks.question: Which of these has the strongest evidence for regrowing hair in pattern hair loss?
options: High-dose biotin
A caffeine 'growth' shampoo
Topical minoxidil
A collagen supplement
blocks.explanation: Topical minoxidil has randomized, placebo-controlled trials in both men and women and is approved without a prescription for pattern hair loss. Biotin helps only if you're deficient, and most growth shampoos and collagen supplements lack controlled evidence.

blocks.label: Check your nutrient basics
blocks.body: Hair loss from deficiency is real but uncommon. The Nutrients track covers iron, vitamin D, zinc and protein — who genuinely runs low, and why megadoses don't help.

lessons.title: Oral health: the daily habits that count
lessons.summary: Fluoride, cleaning between teeth, electric brushes — and what gum disease really has to do with your heart and blood sugar.

blocks.label: of US adults aged 30 and over had periodontitis — infection that destroys the gum and bone holding teeth in place — in a national dental examination survey. Most cases weren't severe, and many people don't know they have it.
blocks.source: Eke et al., Journal of Dental Research 2012

blocks.heading: Fluoride is the proven part
blocks.body:
Tooth decay happens when mouth bacteria turn sugars into acid. Fluoride helps enamel resist that acid and repair early damage. A Cochrane review of 70 trials in children and adolescents found fluoride toothpaste prevented about a quarter of decayed, missing or filled tooth surfaces compared with non-fluoride paste, with bigger effects at higher concentrations and more frequent use (Marinho et al., 2003).

- Brush **twice a day for about two minutes** with fluoride toothpaste — for adults, UK NHS guidance is **1,350–1,500 ppm** fluoride.
- **Spit, don't rinse** afterward, so fluoride stays on your teeth.
- Replace your brush or brush head every 3–4 months, or sooner if the bristles splay.
- How *often* you have sugar matters as much as how much.
- Children have their own guidance: a smear or rice-grain amount under age 3, a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6.

blocks.title: Cleaning between teeth — honest about the evidence
blocks.simple: A toothbrush can't reach between teeth, which is where gum disease and decay often start. Floss, interdental brushes or a water flosser all help. The evidence is weaker than most people assume — but the habit is cheap, low-risk, and your dentist can see the difference.
blocks.mechanism: Plaque left between teeth inflames the gums (gingivitis). In susceptible people, months to years of that inflammation can progress to periodontitis: pockets form, the bone around teeth is lost, and teeth loosen. Interdental brushes clean the wider gaps many adults have better than floss; floss suits tight contacts.
blocks.studies: A 2019 Cochrane review (Worthington et al.) found low- to very-low-certainty evidence that adding floss or interdental brushes to toothbrushing reduces gingivitis or plaque in the short term, with interdental brushes possibly more effective than floss. Evidence on water flossers was limited and inconsistent, and there was too little data on tooth decay. 'Low certainty' mostly reflects small, short trials in people with mild gum inflammation — not proof that cleaning between teeth doesn't work.

blocks.prompt: In a classic 1965 experiment, volunteers with healthy gums stopped all tooth cleaning. Within about how many days did they develop gingivitis?
blocks.explanation: Every volunteer developed gingivitis within 9–21 days without oral hygiene, and their gums returned to health after they resumed cleaning (Löe et al., Journal of Periodontology 1965). The experiment established plaque as the cause of gingivitis. Gingivitis is reversible; the bone loss of periodontitis is not.

blocks.title: Choosing your tools

nodes.label: Electric vs manual brush
nodes.detail: A Cochrane review of 56 trials found powered brushes reduced plaque by 11% at 1–3 months and 21% after 3 months, and gingivitis by 6% and 11%, compared with manual brushing (Yaacob et al., 2014). A manual brush used well for two minutes is still fine; a powered one helps most people do better.

nodes.label: Toothpaste
nodes.detail: Fluoride is the active that matters. Whitening pastes mostly remove surface stains with abrasives. Sensitivity pastes use potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride. Nano-hydroxyapatite pastes have a few promising trials, several industry-funded; fluoride has decades of evidence.

nodes.label: Floss, interdental brushes, water flossers
nodes.detail: Interdental brushes where they fit, floss for tight contacts, a water flosser if braces, implants or limited dexterity make the others hard. The best tool is the one you'll use every day.

nodes.label: Mouthwash
nodes.detail: Not a substitute for brushing. Fluoride rinses can help people prone to decay — use them at a different time from brushing. Strong antiseptic rinses such as chlorhexidine are short-term tools a dentist may recommend; in a small study, a week of chlorhexidine rinse suppressed nitrate-reducing mouth bacteria and raised blood pressure by 2–3.5 mmHg (Kapil et al., Free Radical Biology and Medicine 2013). Daily antiseptic rinsing without a reason isn't clearly beneficial.

nodes.label: Tongue cleaning
nodes.detail: May reduce bad breath in the short term; the evidence is limited.

blocks.title: Gums and the rest of you: what's established
blocks.body: **Diabetes:** the link runs both ways, and it's the best-supported. A 2022 Cochrane review of 35 trials found treating periodontitis lowered HbA1c by about 0.4 percentage points at 3–4 months, with moderate-certainty evidence (Simpson et al.). **Heart disease:** consistently associated, but the American Heart Association has concluded that cause and effect hasn't been established, and there's no evidence gum treatment prevents heart attacks or strokes. Look after your gums for your teeth and blood sugar; treat the heart benefit as unproven.

blocks.question: Your gums bleed when you brush. What's the best response?
options: Avoid brushing the bleeding areas until they stop
Keep cleaning those areas gently and thoroughly, including between the teeth — and see a dentist if the bleeding hasn't settled within a couple of weeks
Replace brushing with an antiseptic mouthwash
Ignore it — bleeding gums are normal
blocks.explanation: Bleeding is the classic sign of gingivitis — inflammation caused by plaque. Avoiding the area lets plaque build up further. Gentle, thorough cleaning usually settles it within a week or two; if it doesn't, see a dentist.

blocks.body: See a dentist for gums that keep bleeding despite good cleaning, swelling, pus, receding gums, loose or shifting teeth, or persistent bad breath. See a dentist or doctor about any mouth ulcer, red or white patch, or lump that hasn't healed within 3 weeks, so oral cancer can be ruled out. Bleeding gums together with easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds or unusual tiredness should be checked by a doctor. Smoking is one of the biggest risk factors for gum disease — and it can hide the bleeding that would warn you.

blocks.label: Browse oral care
blocks.body: On the oral-care shelf, check the fluoride content (ppm) of toothpastes, and whether a mouthwash is a fluoride rinse or an antiseptic — they do different jobs.

lessons.title: Body care, deodorant & fragrance
lessons.summary: Moisturize smart, exfoliate less than you think, and know what your deodorant and perfume actually do.

blocks.heading: Dry skin: draw water in, then seal it
blocks.body:
Moisturizers work through three kinds of ingredients:

- **Humectants** draw water into the skin — glycerin, urea, hyaluronic acid, lactic acid.
- **Emollients** smooth the rough gaps between skin cells — plant oils, squalane, fatty alcohols.
- **Occlusives** form a film that slows water loss — petrolatum, dimethicone, mineral oil, shea butter. Petrolatum is among the most effective, and allergy to it is very rare.

Apply within a few minutes of bathing, on damp skin. Keep showers short and warm rather than hot. For thick, rough skin on heels and elbows, **urea** at higher strengths softens and loosens the buildup.

blocks.title: Exfoliation has a ceiling
blocks.body: Skin sheds on its own. Occasional gentle exfoliation smooths rough patches — and chemical exfoliants such as lactic acid or urea are often gentler than gritty scrubs. But daily scrubbing, stiff brushes and stacked acids break down the barrier and cause dryness, redness and itching. A couple of times a week is a sensible ceiling for most people; for sensitive or eczema-prone skin, often none at all.

blocks.title: Deodorant vs antiperspirant

nodes.label: Deodorant
nodes.detail: A cosmetic. It doesn't reduce sweat — it masks odor and uses antimicrobials, alcohol or fragrance to curb the skin bacteria that break sweat down into smelly compounds.

nodes.label: Antiperspirant
nodes.detail: An OTC drug in the US. Aluminum salts form temporary plugs in sweat ducts, and the product has to prove in testing that it reduces sweat. Many products are both deodorant and antiperspirant.

nodes.label: Apply at night
nodes.detail: Antiperspirant works best on dry skin at bedtime, when sweat glands are quieter and the plugs have time to form. It keeps working after a morning shower.

nodes.label: Why you smell
nodes.detail: Fresh sweat is nearly odorless. Odor comes from bacteria such as Corynebacterium breaking down compounds in underarm sweat. A variant of the ABCC11 gene, common in East Asian populations, sharply reduces underarm odor — and also produces dry earwax.

nodes.label: Aluminum-free switches
nodes.detail: There's no evidence your armpits need to 'detox' when you switch. Baking-soda deodorants are alkaline and can irritate underarm skin.

blocks.prompt: To be labeled 'extra effective', how much must a US antiperspirant reduce sweating in standardized testing?
blocks.explanation: Under FDA's antiperspirant rules, a standard product must cut sweat by at least 20%, and an 'extra effective' one by at least 30%. So even a good antiperspirant reduces sweat rather than stopping it — which is why truly heavy sweating needs a clinician, not a stronger stick.

blocks.heading: Fragrance: pleasant, and a leading allergen
blocks.body:
Fragrance is one of the most common causes of allergic skin reactions to cosmetics. Allergy develops after repeated exposure — often years of trouble-free use — and once it develops it's usually lifelong.

- **Natural isn't safer.** Essential oils such as lavender, tea tree, citrus and ylang-ylang contain the same allergens, and some components (linalool, limonene) become more allergenic as they oxidize in air.
- **Citrus oils plus sun** can cause a reaction: bergamot oil can leave streaky brown marks where perfume was sprayed on sun-exposed skin.
- **Leave-on matters more than rinse-off.** Choose fragrance-free lotions first if you're sensitive; a scented body wash is on your skin for a minute.
- **Spray on clothes, not skin,** if you love a perfume but react to it (test fabric first for staining).

blocks.question: You switch to an 'all-natural' deodorant with essential oils and baking soda, and your underarms turn red and itchy. What's the likely cause?
options: Your body 'detoxing' from aluminum
Irritation from the alkaline baking soda, or an allergy to fragrance compounds in the essential oils
Not applying enough product
Sweat trapped by leftover aluminum
blocks.explanation: Baking soda's high pH is a common irritant for thin underarm skin, and essential oils are fragrance allergens like any other. 'Detox' isn't a real process here. Switch to a fragrance-free, baking-soda-free product; if the rash persists or spreads, see a clinician.

blocks.body: See a clinician if sweating soaks through clothes or disrupts daily life — it's treatable with prescription-strength antiperspirants, other prescription topicals and injections. Get new night sweats checked promptly, especially with fever or unexplained weight loss, because they can signal an underlying illness. A rash that keeps returning where you apply a product is worth a dermatologist's patch test to pinpoint the allergen. And ask a doctor before using antiperspirants if you have kidney disease.

blocks.label: Browse body care & fragrance
blocks.body: Compare moisturizers by their humectants and occlusives, check whether a 'deodorant' is actually an antiperspirant (in the US it will carry a Drug Facts panel), and look for fragrance-free options if your skin reacts easily.

lessons.title: Your personal-care protocol
lessons.summary: The few habits with the most evidence, where to spend vs save, and when to see a dermatologist or dentist.

blocks.heading: Most of the benefit from a few habits
blocks.body: If you remember nothing else from this track: **daily sunscreen**, **fluoride toothpaste twice a day** and **cleaning between your teeth** have the strongest evidence for protecting your health. A **retinoid** is the best-supported add-on for aging skin. Much of the rest is comfort and preference — fine to enjoy, not worth worrying about.

blocks.title: Your starter protocol
items: Morning: gentle cleanse or rinse, moisturizer if needed, then a full dose of broad-spectrum SPF 30+ on face, neck and ears.
Outdoors: reapply every 2 hours; add shade, a hat and sunglasses around midday.
Evening: cleanse, one active if you use one (a retinoid is the best-studied), then moisturizer.
Teeth: fluoride toothpaste for two minutes twice a day, spit don't rinse, and clean between teeth once a day.
Body: short warm showers, moisturizer on damp skin, fragrance-free if you react easily.
Once a month: check your skin, including your back and scalp (use a mirror or a partner), for new or changing spots.
Don't smoke: it speeds skin aging and is one of the biggest risk factors for gum disease.

blocks.title: Where to spend vs save

nodes.label: Save: cleanser
nodes.detail: It's on your skin for under a minute. Gentle and fragrance-free beats expensive.

nodes.label: Save: basic moisturizer
nodes.detail: Glycerin, petrolatum, dimethicone and ceramides are inexpensive ingredients, and pharmacy moisturizers are often just as effective as luxury ones.

nodes.label: Spend more where it makes you actually use it: sunscreen
nodes.detail: Price doesn't predict protection, but texture and feel predict whether you'll wear a full dose every day. Pay for the one you'll actually use.

nodes.label: Spend on evidence: actives
nodes.detail: Pay for a disclosed concentration, protective packaging (opaque, airless or pump for vitamin C and retinoids) and a formula you tolerate — not for exotic extracts.

nodes.label: Worth it: powered toothbrush & interdental brushes
nodes.detail: Modest cost, with trial evidence for less plaque and gingivitis.

nodes.label: Skip: most growth shampoos, biotin, 'detox' products
nodes.detail: Weak or no evidence for people who aren't deficient.

blocks.title: The ABCDEs of moles
blocks.body: **A**symmetry — the two halves don't match. **B**order — ragged, notched or blurred. **C**olor — several shades, or uneven. **D**iameter — larger than about 6 mm, though melanomas can be smaller. **E**volving — changing in size, shape or color, or starting to itch or bleed. Also watch for the 'ugly duckling': a spot that looks different from all your other moles.

blocks.prompt: In the ABCDE rule, a mole wider than about how many millimeters deserves a closer look?
blocks.explanation: About 6 mm, roughly the size of a pencil eraser. But 'Evolving' is the most important letter, and early melanomas can be smaller than 6 mm. Any spot that's new, changing, or unlike your others is worth showing a clinician.

blocks.body: **See a dermatologist or doctor promptly for:** a new or changing mole or spot; a spot that bleeds, itches or crusts; a sore that doesn't heal within a few weeks; a new dark streak under a nail. **See a dentist for:** gums that keep bleeding, swollen or receding gums, loose teeth, or a mouth ulcer, lump or patch lasting 3 weeks. The US Preventive Services Task Force (2023) found insufficient evidence for routine full-body skin screening in adults without symptoms — but that doesn't apply if you have a changing spot, many or unusual moles, a family history of melanoma, previous skin cancer or a weakened immune system. If any of those fit, ask about regular checks.

blocks.heading: The levers upstream of your skin
blocks.body: Personal care sits on top of the rest of your health. Smoking speeds skin aging and gum disease. Sleep shows on your face: in a small experiment, strangers rated people photographed after a night of sleep deprivation as less healthy and more tired than the same people after normal sleep (Axelsson et al., BMJ 2010). And skin, hair and gums are built from what you eat — deficiencies such as low vitamin C or iron can show up there.

blocks.question: Which habit has randomized-trial evidence for reducing skin cancer AND slowing visible skin aging?
options: A daily antioxidant serum
Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen
Collagen supplements
Monthly facials
blocks.explanation: The Nambour trial randomized adults to daily sunscreen and found fewer squamous-cell carcinomas, fewer melanomas in long-term follow-up, and no detectable increase in skin aging over 4.5 years. No serum, supplement or facial has comparable evidence.

blocks.label: Continue with the Sleep track
blocks.body: Your skin's overnight repair runs on the same sleep that restores the rest of you. The Sleep track covers how much you need and the levers that improve it — and the personal-care shelf is under Personal Care whenever you're ready to shop.
